speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall avail myself of this opportunity to reply to the inquiry made by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) on Tuesday with regard to the treaty signed at Washington on the 11th of April last for the marking of the boundaries between Canada and the United States. The hon. gentleman stated that in the last draft of the treaty there was a departure from the wording of the Ashburton treaty. I have to say to the hon. gentleman that the parliamentary paper from which he cited contains a misprint. The article in the treaty says that :
The line shall not intersect islands lying along its course.
These are the terms of the treaty as negotiated in 1900. In the parliamentary paper brought down on the 19th of May last, paper No. 54-A, there is a misprint. The word ' not ' was dropped, but in all the other papers the word ' not ' is included. Sessional paper No. 54-B with regard to the same question, brought down in June last, has the wording correctly. The word ' not ' is in and the treaty reads :
The line shall not intersect islands lying along its course.
That is exactly the wording of the treaty as it was signed at Washington and therefore all the apprehensions of my hon. friend are absolutely without foundation.

In connection with the Waterways treaty, which has not yet been presented to this House, although

what purports to be a copy has been published in the press of the country, I would point out that the treaty seems to have been discussed by one of the commissioners instrumental in negotiating it, Mr. Gibbons, at a recent meeting in the province of Ontario. I observe by the Toronto ' Globe ' of the 23rd inst., that Mr. George C. Gibbons addressed the Canadian Club at Toronto and in the course of his address spoke pretty definitely of some of the terms of the treaty. It does seem to) me under the circumstances that the Prime Minister should expedite the presentation of that treaty to parliament. The terms of the treaty have been made public not only in the United States but in the press of our own country. In addition to that, one of the commissioners who negotiated the treaty feels himself at liberty to discuss its terms. It is little better than a farce that the treaty should not be presented officially to this parliament. I trust that there will he no great delay. I do not know that any great discussion in parliament will be necessary; I assume there will be some discussion, but I merely desire to emphasize the point that parliament ought to be in a position to discuss the treaty when it is being discussed in the press of the country and even by a gentleman who, acting on behalf of this government, was instrumental in framing its terms.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister).
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can inform my hon. friend, by authority, that the treaty has not been communicated officially by the United States to Congress. It has been, of course, submitted to the Senate, which body, under the terms of the constitution, must pass upon it; but it has not been officially communicated to Congress itself. We have been pressing, as fast as we can, to have authority to put it at once upon the table of the House, because I agree with my hon friend in saying that there is no reason that I can see why this should not be done. But he knows that in this matter we are bound by certain rules which we must follow. We are pressing it and hope to have the matter decided at an early day.
How about Mr. Gibbons?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is discussing the treaty as he finds it in the press, I suppose.

I would call attention to the statement made the night before last as we were adjourning. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) told us that we should go into Supply, and that the Minister of Railways and Canals would ask the attention of the committee to his canal estimates. I do not know whether other hon. gentlemen apprehended that as I did, but I understood that we should probably have the pleasure of listening to an address by the Minister of Railways and Canals on the subject of canals, and in that way, we should have the advantage of knowing, perhaps, what is the general, up-to-date policy of the department upon the development of our canal system and other matters connected with that general question.

It has been the custom, I believe, for the Minister of Railways and Canals to make a statement concerning the Intercolonial Railway before we go into Supply. I am not asking to-day for any supply for the railways branch, and will not do so until I am prepared to make a statement to the House. Last year, in discussing the question of transportation, I dealt with the canals incidentally, and, in the few remarks I may make again, I shall mention them.

For years it has been customary for the minister to make a statement on the subject of the Intercolonial. But, the other night, the Minister of Finance specially spoke of the question of canals, and I thought a new departure had been made, and, as the question of canals in Canada is a very important one in connection with the whole problem of trans-

portation, that the minister had determined, on this occasion, to give us interesting information as to what he proposed in reference to the canal system. There are some very interesting features in connection with that question, and some very large promises have been made. I do not know how the other members view the matter, hut I should have been glad if the minister had made a general statement.

We must have a statement, especially as there is a recommendation by the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals in regard to our canal transportation system. He tells us in this report what he thinks is the best system of water communication. We also had a statement from the premier when he was in Welland of what he intended to do in refer-*ence to canals, not only to deepen the Welland canal into Lake Ontario, but in the near future he was going to build the Georgian Bay canal. But the deputy of the department, no doubt voicing the opinion of the department, has proposed a policy. This may not be the proper time to discuss the statement of the minister, but certainly we may expect a statement of the policy of the government.

The House may remember that I gave at some length my opinion on the question of water transportation the other night when on some other estimates. It is well understood, however, that for the present at least, the policy of the government has been pretty well decided on, and it would be unwise to change it in reference to any new undertaking. Those works that are under way will be proceeded with. But I am not retracting from anything I have said as to the desirability of extending our transportation facilities by water. The policy of the government will scarcely be to undertake any new work this year which would mean a large expenditure of money. I may reiterate what every nerson knows to be true, that the great safety valve for our transportation is the development of our waterways. We have the best waterways in the world, and they are canable of the highest development of any waterways in the world. My own opinion is, and I have often expressed it in this House before, that with the Welland canal deepened or a new Welland canal, which would be still better, we can favourably compete with our friends across the line in the carrying trade from the west to the east and in a large measure from the east to the west. That is a large problem. The question of the Georgian Bay canal has been before the House for years, and while opinions are somewhat divided, there seems to be a strong opinion in important circles that that would solve the problem of the carrying trade from the west to the east. However, while I in no way. detract from anything I have said, for the.
present at least the government policy will be not to undertake any of these great works that will call for a large expenditure of money.
Is that policy of progress for the future near at hand, or is it a little less remote than it was in October last?
By the efflux of time it gets closer.
But the ministerial idea does not seem to be as clear as it was in October.
Mine is.

The Minister of Public Works, when he was introducing his estimates stated that a new rule of economy was adopted in his department. I wanted to know whether that prevails in other departments, and perhaps my hon. friend will be able to advise the committee on that point.

The Department of Railways and Canals has always been pretty economical so far as I know. As to details, I was not here when my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works made his remark. But the Department of Railways and Canals is conducted on the most economical lines consistent with the efficiency of the service and the interest of the country.

The Minister of Railways has made an explanation in reference to the contract for cement. Will he explain how it comes that he paid, as shown by the Auditor General's Report, W -9, the Canadian Portland Cement Company, limited, for 5,000 barrels of Star cement at $2.62J; to W. McNally & Company, Portland cement, 2,500 barrels at $2.40. Were these purchased by tender?
They were all purchased by tender. In our department no cement is purchased in any other way.
Has cement fallen so much in the last year?
I think cement has never been so cheap in Canada as it is at the present time.
What is it worth?
$1.12 to $1.20 net, when sold in quantities. By net I mean 10 per cent off when the bag is returned.
Has the minister abandoned the patronage list, like some of the other departments? I do not need to remirid the House of the trouble we had last year in this regard.

I have no recollection of trouble in my department about the patronage list. I think my hon. friend has got mixed up. As a matter of fact, in Some

instances we purchased from a list, on invitation by circular letter. We have notified our various branches that any person who desires is at liberty to tender for any of our goods. If any member, of the House knows of any person that he would like us to ask to tender for any materials that we buy, where the amount is not large enough to warrant us to advertise, we would be delighted to give him a change to tender.
When did that plan originate?
We have always had on that list men of both political parties.
Does the minister intend to do his advertising only in Liberal papers, or in the press generally?

As long as men are human-and I agree with Judge Cassels in this-everything, being equal, it is natural to express confidence in those who have implicit confidence in us so long as the country gets full value for its money. That we insist on in every case.
Could the hon. gentleman give us one instance where a Conservative got a contract? It might be a relief to us if we knew of one case where a Conservative sold goods to the government.

I can give my hon. friend one instance. Perhaps I should not take liberty'with the name, but as he has asked me so pointedly I may say that only a week ago I got a verbal reminder that I had given a large contract for ties to a gentleman who ran against the hon. member for Westmoreland. He got the contract on strict business principles.
Who tendered fpr this cement on page W-9, where you paid $2.62 for 5,000 barrels?
What work is that on?
The Lachine canal. It seems strange that you would pay $2.6%, when you could have purchased it for $1.85 in Ottawa.
That is not correct. $2.62 would probably be the gross price anyway.
Would the minister explain how it is that he requires $40,030 worth of cement on a $250,000'contract? It seems an enormous sum.
I am advised by the engineer that that will not nearly do the work.
In a $250,000 contract?
A largb share of the work is concrete work.

If the minister will turn to page W-14 of the Auditor General's Report, he will find that he purchased from Mr. GRAHAM.
the Colonial Portland Cement Company 2,000 barrels of cement at $1.80, the same year, less 10 cents for sacks; from the Lake-field Portland Cement Company, 2,500 barrels at $2.30; from the Lakefield Portland Cement Company, 212 barrels at $2.30; and yet he paid $2,624 at the Lachine canal, close to where the cement is made. It appears that this cement is all bought just on the job plan, no tenders being invited but simply a circular letter sent out to one or two of the friends of the government.
Mr,. GRAHAM. My hon). friend will agree with me that a year ago cement was much higher than it is now, but I assure him that the cement is all bought by tender, and we give the contract to the lowest tenderer in every instance.
Who tendered when this contract was awarded at $2,624?
That is a year ago; I will have to look it up.
There was a purchase made at the same time at $1.80.
Not at the same time.
Within the same year.
That may be.

When the minister asks for tenders for a very large quantity of cement and gets bids, such as he got here of $2,624, does he cause inquiries to be made whether other large buyers of that article are paying as much as the price mentioned in the tender that he has received, or does he go it blind and, when he gets four or five tenders, just take the lowest?
The department keeps pretty close track of prices by watching the markets and making inquiries, and we think we are buying as cheaply or a little, more cheaply than most people do.

How are these inquiries made? For instance, you have a tender for $40,000 worth of cement; do you inquire what large buyers are paying at that moment, and, if you make these inquiries, are they made by letter?

My deputy informs me that he makes inquiries from big dealers and contractors to see what they are paying; and that he keeps himself posted all the time as to the prices they are paying. He assures me that he is constantly buying cement as cheaply or cheaper than the large buyers.
Are these inquiries made verbally, or are they made by letter, and, if by letter, has the minister any objection to the committee seeing them?

My deputy tells me that he does not recall whether he has done that

in writing or not, but he assures me that it is a fact.
Where is the Canadian Cement Company located?
At Marlbank and at Port Colborne. The difference in freight charges might make some difference in prices.
Will not the cement companies have uniform prices throughout Canada?

Last year they did approximate closely to a uniform price, and I assured one of the large dealers and so informed the officials that if there was any evidence at all that these men are combining to charge us unduly for cement we would ask for tenders from outside; we would not be held up, but on investigation, I believe we are buying cement this year as cheaply as any one and perhaps a little cheaper.
I suppose you are very careful to see that the cement is of the quality specified by the department?
Yes, we have it tested.
There was to be a reason given why these amounts were chargeable to capital instead of income.

This is practically new work.
Lachine canal-To stop leaks on north bank at Cote St. Paul, $29,000.

I might as well make an explanation. These banks have proved not to be entirely safe. What we are doing is practically making a new portion of the bank of concrete in order that it may be absolutely safe. We propose to put a concrete slab 18 inches thick in front of these walls. The break in the Cornwall canal has led me to say to the deputy minister and chief engineer to take no chances of such a thing occurring again if it is in our power to prevent it. Wherever we find that a canal bank has been leaking we put a slab of concrete along the bank to prevent such a thing happening again.

When was the contract made?
On December 12, 1908.
Has the department taken any means of ascertaining whether the price is reasonable?

We always insist that our own engineer shall make an estimate in order to ascertain whether the price is reasonable or not before we accept a tender. Our chief engineer is our authority for saying the price is reasonable before it is approved.
When was this contract advertised and when were the tenders to be in?
Advertised on 14th October; tenders to be in at 16 o'clock, Thursday, 22nd October.
It looks suspicious to have all these tenders received two or three days before the election.
We were trying to do this work at the close of navigation; it had nothing to do with the election.
I should think the minister would be too busy about that time to attend to these matters.
So far as I am personally concerned I was.
The 22nd of October might be considered a bargain day for contracts.
I should think the minister would be very busy at home just then.	1
Not at home, but elsewhere.
What is the nature of the foundation?
They make a trench in the clay bank and they fill in from that trench the 18-inch slab along the face of the wall.
The foundation does not go below the bottom of the canal?
Just sufficient to cut off any leakage.
Could not this work be done when the water was out of the canal?
I do not like to say it too loudly, but it would be a very dangerous experiment to unwater the Soulanges canal; the chief engineer has reported it must not be done.
It is a clay bottom and when the water is out there would be danger of the clay coining up?

Yes.
Chambly canal-St. Johns harbour improvements, $44,000.
There were eight tenders ; the contract is dated December 15, and it went to the lowest tender.
Who was that?
John G. Poupore & Co.
Will this vote finish the work?
It is schedule rate; the approximate sum given in the contract is $35,282. The engineer would not be positive this will complete the work but he thinks it probably will.
I suppose the increased traffic from St. Johns on the Chambly canal necessitates this work?

It has been asked for years. Complaint was made to me that the harbour was so crowded that they simply could notl do the business they had to do. We had difficulty in getting a title to the property or it would have been done before.
Ontario-St. Lawrence canals-District office. $7,000.
Where is that?

This is not the staff that has charge of the canal. This is the staff that has1 had charge of the construction of the new canals and improvements on the St. Lawrence river. N. L. Rheaume is in charge, and they have an office, with electric lights, telephone, &c., and they are making the final estimates.

As I understand, {he works on the St. Lawrence canals are practically through, with the exception of one little work at the head of the Galops canal. Yet this office has been kept there for years, with the same staff. How long will they be kept there?
We have put all our men in this office. The winding up does seem to be an arduous process, but we hope shortly to get the final estimates made.
Is this vote for building an office for them?
No, we are not building any office. It is just for the salaries of the men.

The final estimate for the Cornwall canal must have been made a year ago. All the works on the St. Lawrence canals must have been completed and paid for. There is only one work going on yet. I cannot understand what that staff is there for.

It depends altogether on the meaning we attach to the term final estimates. What we are requiring of these men is to make not only a final estimate as to cost, but a record of everything in connection with these canals, consisting of drawings in full, detail of the finished structure, to which we can refer, and which will give us a clear insight into every part of these canals at any time in the future.

The hon. minister knows that the men made these records from time to time as the work went along, and when the final estimate was made they had the plans and everything completed in the most minute way. In addition, I understand, the measurements were sent to the department here, where there are engineers making plans for future reference.
I think that all the information the hon. minister refers to is here in the department.

My deputy informs me that the plans are not all made here. Tha engineers use the plans and specifications in the construction of the work, and when that is done they are required to make re-drawings of the completed structure, which are put in bound form and sent to the department. For instance, in the case of the Soulanges canal, the men who were

engaged on it are all dead and if we had not a complete record of that work in the form of the plans and specifications we would have been in a predicament now in regard to that canal. This is costing a little money, but we are getting a complete and accurate record of all these canals.

I admit that it is absolutely necessary to have a complete record; but it should not take more than a year for that staff to make such a record as the hon. minister refers to. The Cornwall canal has been completed for three or four years, the Williamsburg canal has been completed for six or seven years, and the other canals have also been completed a long time. I am not finding fault with an expenditure for the purpose of getting such records as the hon. minister refers to. In that respect I believe he is absolutely right; but it is common talk along the canal that there are a number of men there who are really not required, and who are simply drawing their pay. I am not mentioning this for the purpose of having these men dismissed from the service of the government; but there are many places, on the Transcontinental Railway and elsewhere, to which they could be removed, and where they would have something to do to earn their salaries. If the minister told these men that they would have to get these records completed in three months, they would do it, provided they were sure of a position somewhere else in the department. But so long as there is nothing in view for them, so long will they remain where they are.

It must strike the hon. minister's common sense that it is somewhat difficult to explain the keeping on of engineers who have drawn the plans of works for which the contracts have been finished and the final estimates made. He is keeping a staff of five or six men after the work is completed, for what purpose ? Recording the manner in which the work was constructed, or the plans or estimates for it? There is no necessity for it whatever. I am in a different position from my hon. friend. These parties have votes in his riding.
No, they are not in my riding at all.
They were, but they are not now.
They are very near it. I cannot understand the necessity for keeping these men on.

I think the trouble arises from the misleading form of the item. This is not an estimate at all according to the minister. The work is all completed and this is a charge for making up a record of the work already done.

I am inclined to agree that without an explanation the words ' final estimate ' would not explain to the committee just what was meant. My deputy has visited the office in Cornwall on several occasions. It is a mistake to say that the work is all completed. Mr. Rheaume has charge of the work going on in the north channel as well as this, but has not been altogether engaged in this work. We hope to get it concluded and we are urging it as rapidly as possible.
Is the $30,000 asked for the removal of the shoal at the upper entrance a final estimate?
It is difficult, as my hon. friend knows, to tell just when you are through with a piece of work of that kind. A boat finds another boulder and the work keeps going on.
Is there any estimate for the dam at Adam's island?
We have no estimate for that
What is the explanation of the entry at page W-92 of the Auditor General's Report, * employees whose duties were materially reduced by the closing of navigation on December 5, 1907 ' ?

Some of the men engaged on the locks in the summer are dropped in the fall. They are not really permanent employees although they are all there every year. If we want a man for instance to watch a weir we utilize one of these men in the slack season.
What are the duties of the collector of tolls on the Galops canal and what are his powers?
I do not think he is called collector of canal tolls. The services of such men are utilized to keep complete records of the canal statistics.
While they do not collect the tolls as formerly they still issue passes to steamers.
It is his duty to be there all the time during navigation.

This man is also collector of customs, and his office as such collector is two miles away. He is supposed to be in regular and constant attendance there. How can the minister expect one man to fill these two places?
I do not know the particulars of the case referred to. This officer's work seems to have been done satisfactorily, for we have had no complaints. However, I will make inquiry.
He is drawing two salaries and doing nothing.
Both make one salary.

The minister knows that for forty years the two offices were at one point, at the locks. But lately the canal office has been moved up about two miles. Of course, a great deal of fault has been found in the county of Grenville at one man occupying two positions when it is impossible for one man to perform the duties of both. There is complaint especially among the Liberals who think that two offices for one man is too large an allowance. The minister says that the salaries are small. The collector of canal tolls has always had a salary of $750 a year, besides this the collector at Cardinal is allowed $1 a day for a horse to drive him up to his office, two miles away. This makes at least $250 a year additional. So, this collector has a higher salary than has been paid since the canal was built. There was another officer who had the position of sub-[DOT]collector of customs at a salary of $400. But when this subcollector of customs was superannuated, the man who held the office of collector of canal tolls was appointed to this office also. As the offices are two miles apart, there is no question that the duties of one position or of the other must suffer. I am not finding fault with the officer at all, but I think the minister should call upon him to make a choice of one office or the other.

So far as the records furnished me show, the salary is $700 a year, and there is no allowance for horse-hire. It seems that this man was the officer of the Bailways and Canals Department and that afterwards the other position was given him. It is not unusual, where the government has two small positions to appoint one man to fill them both. One salary, especially that from the customs would be rather small. I suppose the reason the canal office has to be further west than before is that the cut-off has been made into the river.

Formerly, the boats had to go through the lock at Cardinal, but, since the new work was built, there is no lock now between Iroquois and the head of the canal. In the case of boats going down the canal, the officer is supposed to issue passes, and, to do this, he needs to be in his office. Otherwise, you do not get a complete record of the commerce through the canal. It can easily be shown whether the records in this respect have been kept in complete form or not. Every vessel from the west passing down to Montreal, and drawing fourteen feet of water, must pass through that lock. They cannot go through the Galops-at least they do not. Of course, a vessel going to Montreal, if no pass is issued at Cardinal, can have a pass issued at Cornwall. But I am satisfied that the work of both these offices is not being pro-Mr. G. TAYLOE.
perly done. Either the government is losing money in the customs collection, or it is losing in the efficiency of its record of canal business. As to the question of horse-hire, for this officer, I am confident that I have seen it in the Auditor General's Ee-port. I have not the figures under my eye at the moment, but I will look up the record and will refer to it later.

I agree that what the department is interested in is having its work well done. It is only just to the official who has been referred to that I should say that there has been no complaint from vesselmen of any lack of attention.

Of course, even if the officer is not at the canal office when a vessel goes through, you will get the record at Cornwall, or, I suppose, it could be had at the Soulanges canal. At the same time, it should be taken at the Galops. I understood the minister to say that he was interested in seeing that the work only of his own department is well done. I think that he is interested as a member of the government in seeing that the work of all the departments is well done. I believe the minister should say to this officer: Either take the position under the Department of Bailways and Canals, and drop the other, or else take the position in the Department of Customs and we will appoint another man to carry on our business. I would ask the minister to look into that, to have that matter put right, so that next session when it comes up again I will not have to draw his attention to the fact that there is one man filling two positions two miles apart.
We are inaugurating a new system of keeping these records that I think will detect in a week any neglect of duty.

I would like the minister to promise me this: If he keeps the collector of canal tolls at Galops canal, he will see that the man is there in person while the canal is open. If he does that, the Minister of Customs will have to have another officer there; and, if he does, I will prove that the revenues will not be received right unless they have a proper officer there.
I will promise to see that this officer does his duty faithfully.
Is it to be done by himself, or how?

I want to call the minister's attention to page W-138: Lock at Cardinal, $1,041. This includes statistical officer, 12 months, $700; sundries, 534 hours at 20c.; conveyance to office, 229 trips at $1. There are 26 days in a month, that would be over eight months. I took it for granted you were allowing him $1 a day for driving two miles up to the office.

My accountant informs me that he had in his hand the winter paylist when he gave me the information a moment ago. He does get a $1 a day for the summer conveyance.
Trent Canal, $1,000,000.

I would like to ask the minister if the contracts that are being let by numbers on the Trent canal number from the south or from the Bay of Quinte end, north or west; that is, No. 1 contract would be at Trenton, No. 2 above, and so on. I would like to know to whom the contract for the construction of No. 1 division was first given.
It is an English firm, I can get the name.
I would like to know the amount of deposit made by that firm with their tender, and what was the amount of their tender?
I have not those papers here, I was using them for a return that the hon. gentleman moved in the House. But I have sent for them.

I would like to know if this million dollar expenditure on the Trent canal has anything to do with the North York extension, which is known as the Aylesworth canal, or the Mulock canal. Under what heading are the exenditures on the canal in North York made
ere?

I imagine the Newmarket canal is the one my hon. friend refers to, it is called the Holland River canal. This million dollars includes all the work on the Trent canals this year, and the Newmarket canal is a portion of the Trent valley work.
What has North York to do with the Trent canal? Does it extend down to North York?

There are few men, unless they have, made a study of this question, who appreciate the extent and importance of the Trent Valley work. It not only involves the large project of constructing the canal but it includes branches leading from Lake Simcoe and from the canal. Notwithstanding that there is considerable
fun poked at this feature of the work let me point out to my hon. friend that the whole Trent Valley canal scheme had as much fun poked at it as has this portion now. But any person who has seriously inquired into the Trent Valley project will agree with me that it is going to be a valuable aid not only to that section of the country but to the country as a whole. There may be differences of opinion as to the branch to which my hon. friend refers, but my engineer has made a report which indicates that even the Newmarket branch will be a very useful adjunct to the trade of the country.
Where are you going to get water from?

There are things we cannot see perhaps because we are not engineers, but competent engineers tell me that there will be a sufficient supply of water by storage and otherwise to make that branch of the Trent canal practicable. Persons living along the canal will understand that it is one continuous system of storage by dams in order to make a sufficient supply of water available for the canal.
What portion of this vote is to be for the Newmarket portion of the system?

It is a little difficult to make the division. We have certain contracts under way. We expect to continue the work now going on, and, except in a smaller degree, we will not undertake any of the larger works this year for reasons that I stated when I began.
An hon. M EMBER. There is no election on now.

No, my hon. friend is mistaken about that. There is a difference of opinion as to whether we ought to curtail even in view of the financial position. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) is very strongly of the opinion that the government ought to branch out rather than curtail. However the policy of the government has been to not discontinue any work that has been undertaken, possibly to undertake some smaller ones, but as far as the larger expenditures are concerned not to launch upon any new ones this year. I think that business men will see the wisdom of that course.

I think this estimate ought to have been put in separately. This is a separate work and entirely distinct from the Trent canal. Three hundred thousand dollars were put through originally for this canal, and what I want to get at is whether that has already been absorbed and whether more is being appropriated in this general vote for the Trent canal.

I will give my hon. friend all the information as to the expen-

diture, contracts and everything else. We keep all the contracts separate, but we take one large vote for the Trent Valley canal, as all theese works are included in that system. You cannot very well make them separate works in a large undertaking oi this kind. Now, in reply to my hon. friend from West Hastings (Mr. Porter), I will read a copy of an order in council as I think it will give him all the particulars that he requires. It is as follows:
Feb. 18, 1908.
On a memorandum dated Feb. 13, 1908, from the Minister of Railways and Canals representing that under the authority of order in council dated the 5th November, 1907, a contract for the construction of section No. 1 Ontario-Rice Lake division of the Trent canal, was awarded to Mr. Louis P. Nott,-
What section is that?
What was the amount?
I will send for the figures. I refused to return the deposit.
Why?
Because he put up a forfeit; he sent a marked cheque with his tender. I refused to return that, saying I believed he ought to forfeit that deposit for refusing to sign the contract.
Was not that a condition of his tender?
Yes, it was a condition of his tender that he would carry out the contract.
Was the fair wage clause also a condition of the tender?

There was the cause of the difficulty. After certain communications, some written and some verbal, the Minister of Justice advised us that under the conditions we could not successfully withstand an action in the Court of Exchequer and that we had better return the cheque. Under that advice we returned his deposit. Why could not we keep the cheque or why did1 the Minister of Justice give us the opinion that we were not entitled to keep it? It was based upon the ground that the advertisement did not contain a clause saying that the contractor must accept the fair wage schedule) in making his contract. That had never been inserted in any advertisement because all our contractors fully understand it. It has been in all our contracts and Canadian contractors understood that if they made a tender for any work they had to accept a fair wage clause in their contract. This being a foreign company they did not know of the requirement, and it not being set out in the advertisement the Department of Justice advised us we could not resist an action which had been taken in the Court of Exchequer, and we returned the deposit.
Before his tender was accepted did he not have access to the form of contract required to be entered into?
Yes.
The advertisement required the contract to he entered into upon the form prescribed by the department so that he had ample opportunity of seeing the form of contract?

It was my contention that he had absolute opportunity to inform himself on that point; that it was his own fault if he did not, and that the cheque should not be returned. But he started his proceeding in the Exchequer Court, and_ the Department of Justice advised us officially that we could not resist it and that we had better return the cheque.

Then we are to understand that although the contractor had full opportunity to know the conditions of the contract before tendering, and the Department of Railways and Canals believing, such being the case, that his deposit should be forfeited, the Minister of Justice in the face of these facts advised that the dmosit should be returned.
That is pretty nearly correctly stated except that we did not hold he had absolute knowledge; we held he had full opportunity to get the knowledge.

He was willing to undertake the construction of these works for $866,000, and no objection was raised by him on the ground that he had taken the contract too low?
_ Mr. GRAHAM. Had he raised that objection it would not of course have been a legal excuse for getting back his deposit. My department is of opinion that he discovered his tender was too low and that that was the real reason why he refused, although technically another reason was given.
Nott & Co. are a well known firm of English contractors and have ample means to carry out any contract they undertake?
No doubt about that.
The department had no fear on that ground?
No.
Then the only objection was to the fair wage clause being in the contract?

The department believes that having found his tender was too low h-* sought for an available way to honourably get out of the contract, and he took the legal stand that the fair wage clause not being in the advertisement he could not be held. On that ground the Deputy Minister of Justice advised that we could not resist the action. I may mention that this tender was $200,000 less than the estimate of our own engineer, and having found that he looked for a means
To get out of his contract.

Yes, to put it in plain English. He no doubt consulted some good lawyer like my hon. friend (Mr. Porter), who apparentlv discovered that he could legally get out of his contract on this plea and the Department of Justice upheld the contention. I may say that in future all advertisements will contain a paragraph saying that the contractor must accept the fair wage clause and hence difficulties of the kind will be obviated.
When did the department decide to return the cheque?
I do not know the date, but it was not returned until the Deputy Minister of Justice gave his opinion and I think that was after the action had been instituted.
It was not returned until after the present contract had been accepted?
I am not sure as to that. Of course the only penalty we could impose was to keep the cheque when he refused to enter into his contract.
There is $1,000,000 included in this item, and I would ask the minister to separate from that lump sum the amounts required for each section of the canal.

There is great difficulty in dividing these items as the hon. gentleman suggests. We want to do the best we can, and if we voted a certain amount for a certain section we could not vary the estimate in any way, and we would not get the full benefit of the $1,000,000 which we intend to expend. If we were to spend two and a half million dollars as the engineers wanted me to do, the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) would not be difficult, but perhaps on one section I would not want to spend all the money voted for it, and on another section I would want to spend more, and if the estimates were given in detail, as suggested, we could not do that. We will distribute the money as well as we possibly can, and we will not delay the work on any section more than is necessary.
On what sections is it intended to do work? There is no use trying to cover a multitude of sins with one vote; let us get down to business.
Sections 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7 are the sections on which we will do work.
Will the hon. minister designate the sections by name ?

No. 1 runs from Trenton about three miles up the river. No. 2, the next section, runs up to the vicinity of Frankfort. No. 3 is from Frankfort to the foot of Bradley bay. No. 5, is the section above Campbellford running as far as Crow bay. No. 7 is from below Hastings to Rice lake. The Newmarket canal is called No. 1 of the Holland river section. The other is the Ontario-Rice lake division.
So that the canal is divided into divisions-the Holland river division and the Ontario-Rice lake division.
Yes.
Can the minister state how this vote is to be divided between the two divisions ?

We have expended thi3 year to date on the Holland river section $182,795.18 and on the Ontario-Rice lake division $852,188.77. The work will be carried on next year in approximately the same proportions between these two divisions.
Did the hon. minister ascertain the amount of the deposits of Nott and Company?
It was an accepted cheque of $20,000.

The advertisement required a certain proportion upon the tender, did it not ?
Mr. GfttAHAM. They put in a certain amount with their tender, and the balance must be put up when the contract is entered into.
Before the contract was let for the construction of No. 1 section, were tenders advertised for again ?

No. We considered, as I think it was fair to do, that this man had not practically a tender in at all. We accept the next lowest, but would not have accepted it if it had not been approximately near to the engineer's estimate.

Does it not appear to the hon. minister that that was not quite fair, when the tender of Nott and Company was accepted ? It was then known generally what the tender of each party was. Nott and Company, a very old and reliable firm of contractors, having tendered for the construction of this work for $866,000 odd, and having put up their cheque for $20,000, would it not appear to the hon. minister, under these circumstances, that it would have been wise to call for new tenders ? Does it not appear to the hon. minister that it would have only been fair to those who did tender to have the same opportunity of tendering as this first man, who practically had two tenders ?
No, he had not.
He had only one tender, but he had two chances, whereas the others had only one chance.

No, they had only the one chance. The difficulty of that would have been that every person would have known what every other person's tender was. If I were building a house and called for tenders, and my architect told me confidentially that one of the tenders was too low, and if the tenderer backed out, I would not think of asking for new tenders if the next tender were from a reliable firm and were considerably lower than the estimate of the architect. In this case, there was so much diversity in the tenders that there could not possibly have been collusion. I want to correct the statement I made to my hon. friend. These people not only sent in their first cheque with the tender, but when they were notified that they had the contract, they sent in an additional amount making a total of $43,333.
Before the second payment was made on their deposit had their attention not been called to the fair wage clause in the contract? I understand it had, that they had full knowledge of it at that time.
Of course we cannot speak from their standpoint, and I would not like to say that they had, but our opinion was that they had every opportunity of having full knowledge of it.
Was that fact brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice?
I think all the facts in our possession were placed before the Justice Department?

I understand that the Minister of Railways and Canals would feel bound to act on the opinion of the Minister of Justice. Does it not appear on the face of it that there was here every opportunity for collusion between these parties? Nott & Company, as the minister says, sought for some means of escaping from this contract, and after having tendered or agreed to enter into it withdrew and as the policy of the department was to accept the next lowest tender in such a case was there not every opportunity for Larkin & Sangster, the second lowest tenderers; to make a bargain with Nott & Company by which the additional amount of nearly $150,000 might be divided between them? Larkin & Sangster might be sure that they could construct this work for at least as small a sum as Nott because they were right on the ground with their plant established, old contractors. Would it not seem as if the wise course for the government would have been to call for tenders a second time and afford every tenderer an equal opportunity and thus protect the interests of the country? Is there any check on the contractors to see that they observe the fair wage clause?

Yes, the fair wage officer of the Labour Department. The fair wage clause is Included in every contract now and if the men employed make a complaint it is the duty of the fair wage officer of the Labour Department to investigate it and if possible adjust the difficulty.
In reference to the advisability of taking the next tender instead of advertising for new tenders, it would be only suspicion that there was any collusion, and after thinking the matter over I concluded that under the circumstances there was no collusion and it would be safe to do this. Our chief engineer gave an estimate of $1,074,000 while Larkin & Sangster tendered for $969,237, so that their tender was away below what our chief engineer said the work would cost. If we took the view of my hon. friend that every tenderer knew what the others were bidding there would have been an opportunity for a great deal stronger collusion than before. The chances are it might have cost the country $500,000 more.
But you were not obliged to accept any tender?

But we wanted the work done and accepted the lowest tender. After consulting with the engineer we concluded that we would not get any lower tender, and as we had received another tender still many thousands less than our own estimate, we decided we had better accept the next tender.	*
Some of these other tenderers who were higher than Larkin & Sangster think they were not treated fairly and that they should also have had two chances?
Larkin & Sangster had only one chance. If the other contractors had been in their place one of them would have got the contract.

The matter has been brought seriously to my attention by complaints of men in the employ of the contractors on section 1 of the construction work of that canal. I am told that notwithstanding the fair wage clause the contractors have been paying the men a less rate than would be considered a fair rate under this clause of the contract and less than men similarly qualified and employed were receiving on other portions of the canal. Although complaints were made no redress was given and when the complaint of the men became too strong for the contractors to stand, a large number of these men were dismissed from the work. It seems to me that if the fair wage clause in the contract is to have any effect and to be of any advantage to the workmen, the department ought to see that it is fairly enforced.
And, if the contractor is violating it, as I am instructed this contractor has done, it should not depend upon the men making a complaint; the Department of Labour should act, having an officer whose duty it is to see that in all public contracts this clause is fairly and properly carried out. One can readily understand that a man who is in the employ of another would hesitate before making a complaint that might have the effect of losing him his job. This provision was enacted by this parliament for the benefit and advantage of labouring men, and the onus ought not to be put upon them of seeing that it is carried out. The officer appointed by the government ought to make it his business, by visiting, consultation or in some other way, to ascertain the facts, and, if necessary, to bring proper pressure to bear upon the contractors to cause them to live up to this clause of the contract. I understand that, in this case, men living in the immediate vicinity of the works on No. 1 division, who were given employment in the first instance, were promised that, after the works got fairly started, the wages would be increased to the rates that would be considered fair wages under the contract. But when the elections were over, they were told they might go back to their homes and quietly remain there for the length of time it was supposed to be necessary to construct the Trent canal, because the contractors could get Hungarians and Italians to work for wages they wanted to pay. This is a direct violation of the contract, and the government should make serious inquiry into it; and, if the facts are as I have been informed they are, should take immediate steps to remedy this wrong.
I would ask the minister also if any policy has been laid down or any determination reached, as to how this canal shall be looked after when construction is completed ? That is, will it be divided into divisions as it has been for the purposes of construction, and a superintendent placed over each division, or wilJ there be one superintendent for the whole system ?

Of course, it is a little difficult to speak so far ahead. Not that I mean to say it will be a long time before this canal will be constructed, but it has been in progress ever since 1833, I believe, and if a man had been asked about the policy then
But everybody is in earnest now.

Yes; to be serious, my opinion now would be that one superintendent ought to be able to look after the canal as a whole, with one overseer of each division. I would not like to lay that down as a policy, but it strikes me that that would be sufficient.

I may tell the hon. minister (Mr. Graham) for his own information-it may not be of much advantage to the government-that in October and early November last, in the town of Trenton, there were at least twenty-five individuals who were to become superintendent of No. 1 division of the Trent canal. I would like to know if the minister had authorized the candidate who opposed me in the election to make promises to these twenty-five or more men I have referred to ?
I am a very careful promiser.

I have no doubt of it. But that does not alter the fact that the promise was made by the candidate of this government in the elections. Before concluding this inquiry, I would like to ask if there is any clause in the contract which compels the contractor to work continuously until the work is completed ?

There is not. Conditions might arise under which we could stop the contractor in his work. There is no clause compelling him to go on with his work continuously, but there is a time limit for

completion of the work, and, as a matter of fact, we do keep him working continuously.

The minister should see to it that candidates for election in support of his party are better instructed, for the promise was made, based upon the assertion that there was a clause in the contract which compelled it, that the contractor would work continuously and that work would be furnished to the labouring men around Trenton all winter. But, again, as soon as the elections were over, the work was stopped-to be commenced again in the spring, I suppose-and the men were laid off. I do not know whether that was the only inducement held out to these men to vote, hut that was one of them in the last election.

I should think that it was a misnomer in these estimates to speak of the appropriation for the work on the Holland river as part of the Trent canal. I cannot understand why it is not set out separately to show exactly what the intent of the administration is in going on with the construction of the Holland river section. I am sure that hon. members on this side were pleased to see the sudden change that came over the ministers in reference to the Trent Valley canal. Prior to 1896, the friends of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) condemned the Trent canal on every platform on which they spoke. This expenditure on the Holland river is the most indefensible appropriation asked for in these estimates. I have the honour to represent a constituency adjoining that of the Minister of Justice, and I venture to express the opinion that if a cabinet minister had not been the representative of North York, there would have been no such expenditure in connection with the Holland river. Ministers, apparently, are vieing with one another in getting large appropriations for their several constituencies. Just before election, a large number of men were employed on this work merely ' from ' considerations of political exigencies, and not because the work is a defensible one or is required in the public interest. If the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) has any regard for his reputation as a minister he will discontinue the expenditure on the Holland river canal. The work is meeting not only the condemnation but the derision of all men who have ' any 1 idea ' as to how ' money should be spent in the public interest. I have a letter from a gentleman who resides in New York, at Newmarket, which is supposed to be the dead end of the canal. It is dated February 20. The writer says :
The only sensible thing which is said about it is that it would have been much cheaper if the government had presented William Cane & Sons with several hundreds of thousands Mr. GRAHAM.
of dollars, as they will be the only people who can possibly profit by the canal.
Now Wm. Cane & Sons are manufacturers in Newmarket, and are prominent workers in the Reform party. They desire an outlet to bring in some raw material in connection with their business, and were it not that Wm. Cane & Sons are prominent Reformers I do not think that this vote would appear in the appropriations, either this year or any other year. Not only are all reasonable men strongly against this expenditure, but the newspapers of the country condemn it, and laugh at it. Every newspaper you pick up, whether Conservative, Reform or Independent, condemns this as a useless expenditure of public money. I desire to direct the attention of the minister to an article that appeared in ' Saturday Night ' just previous to the last general election. As the minister knows, ' Saturday Night ' is a paper with independent leanings, neither Conservative nor Reform, and it is a pretty well informed paper. On September 12, 1908, it had this editorial:
It is almost a pity that the work on the new canal to Newmarket-the new canal which is almost to make Newmarket an ocean port-could not be screened off from view from the car windows until it is finished. Passengers on the trains discuss the enterprise with levity. They speak of it as a canal on which nothing but votes will be floated. They express doubt as to where the water will come from to supply the canal, until one passenger explains that the difficulty has been solved by an arrangement whereby it will be hauled in carts from Lake Simcoe. People who know nothing about engineering should not presume to discuss in this fashion a great public work, and in order to prevent this flippant discussion, a screen should be built to shut away the view from passing trains until the elections are over and the frosts of winter cause operations to cease for the present.
Now I appeal to the judgment of the minister if he does not think it proper in the public interest to discontinue an expenditure of thi3 kind. It is absolutely useless. It is only put in the estimates for the purpose of fulfilling some pre-election pledges made on behalf of friends of the government. It does not serve any useful public purpose. Under these circumstances I cannot but condemn the appropriation. Then there is another newspaper in Orillia which deals with this matter. Orillia is situated on Lake Simcoe, and the paper has consequently accurate knowledge of the facts. The article is too long to read. I would refer the minister to this extract which appears in the ' Orillia Packet ' of February 18, 1909 :
In answer to a question by Mr. Currie, the Minister of Railways submitted to the House a table of gaugings made at Newmarket in 1907 relative to the flow of water over the weir. The measurements had to do with the

construction of the proposed canal, and showed that from July to November the average flow was about 540 cubic feet a minute. It ranged from 313 cubic feet in August to 885 in November.
When one remembers that the average water-wagon contains about 150 cubic feet, the terrific intensity of the roar created by this appalling cataract may be understood. The wisdom of the government in passing the appropriation for this canal before taking the gaugings cannot be too highly commended. Perhaps if the gaugings had been taken first the vote would not have been made and the political interests of North York would have suffered.
The mere fact that there is not enough water to fill the canal might be embarrassing to an ordinary administration, but the Lau-rier government is not ordinary. It laughs at impossibilities. Mr. Graham says that storage reservoirs will be required to utilize the spring freshets as a feeder during the summer months. How many storage reservoirs will be required no one says. But no matter how many, they must be built. The transportation requirements of the country demand that Newmarket be made a seaport, and the political requirements of the Minister of Justice demand a canal of some kind wherein the glad electors can fish for mud-cats and meditate on the glories of the government.
This, no doubt, is a charming picture, but it is subject to amendment. Even with storage reservoirs the mud-cat might find the going rather hard. Some person might throw a salmon can into the canal and cause a shoal whereon many virtuous fish might run aground. A good deal may be said in favour of the Newmarket canal by those who do not know what they are talking about. It certainly will have one great advantage. No bridge will be needed. If a North York elector has occasion to cross this noble waterway he can put on his rubbers.
Now I say again, in view of these protests made, one by an independent paper and the other by a paper situated on Lake Simcoe, with full knowledge of the facts, I say the minister should satisfy himself of the urgency of this expenditure before he asks us to vote hundreds and hundreds of thousands of the people's money. It is a shame and a scandal that the public moneys of Canada should be spent in this way, in order to advance the political interests of a member of the government. I say further that an appropriation of this kind should not be allowed to go through. We do not know what expenditure is going to be involved on this Holland river division, nor on the Trent canal division. It is put in here under the broad heading of Trent canal, and has absolutely nothing to do with the Trent canal. And why they disguise the appropriation under the heading of the Trent canal, I cannot tell, except it be that the hon. gentleman is probably ' preparing ' a way to defend past appropriations for the Trent canal. He says the Trent canal is a useful public expenditure. That is not what the hon. gentleman and his
friends said prior to 1896. But now he is willing to defend this canal, and consequently he makes the Holland river division, or the Aylesworth division ditch, as it is called in that region of country, a part of the Trent canal in order to cover up the whole enterprise. 1 say the policy of the government is worthy of the severest condemnation of this committee, and it should not be allowed to go through without a division, in order that the government and their supporters may go on record. The minister does not say what the work is going to cost, he does not say where it is going to end. He laughs at the whole project, and says it was started away back in 1830 and he does not see an end to it. When are we going to see an end of the Holland river canal, or the Aylesworth ditch? Even the honest Reformers of North York are condemning this expenditure. There is not a reasonable Reformer in North York that would justify it. The Minister of Justice is losing his influence in consequence of his advocacy of this ridiculous expenditure. We find that there are men in every town in North York who have public contracts from the government in consequence of this expenditure; we find the government expending $300,000 or $400,000 in order to ensure the return of the Minister of Justice. I say the Minister of Justice is losing his influence in his own constituency in consequence of this expenditure. He came into my constituency and spoke on one occasion, with the result that his influence proved less than nil, because the Conservative majority was increased threefold, showing that he is losing his influence. Now I appeal to the good judgment and fair common sense of the minister to withdraw this appropriation for the Holland river division. I may say frankly that I have always had a great respect for the good judgment of the Minister of Railways and Canals. He is only inheriting the sins of his predecessors, because I do not think that he himself would have initiated a scheme of this kind. But he now feels it incumbent upon himself to continue an expenditure that was inaugurated by his predecessors. I would say with that gentleman who wrote that letter from Newmarket that the expenditure is unjustifiable, and it would be a good thing for the country if the government would hand over to Wm. Cane & Sons a bonus of $350,000, and stop this work. I submit that the minister should give us the details of what he proposes to expend on this canal next year, before he asks us to adopt this vote.
What is the estimated cost of this part of the Trent Valley canal?

We spent about $183,000 on this portion of the canal last year, and we spent $800,000 on the other portion. I told my hon. friend that the expenditure

this year would practically be in the game proportion. We are taking a small vote for the entire work, and I want to have every dollar available without absolutely tieing it up to any particular section. One contract is made for this portion and there are contracts for three other portions, and the money will be expended probably in the same proportion that it was last year. We spent a trifle over $1,000,000 last year, and the same amount of money will probably be expended this year.

I wish to make a protest against this useless expenditure in North York. I agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe); I think this item should be stricken out of the estimates. This is an absolutely useless expenditure, and I do not think the vote should go through.
The minister did not answer the question of my hon. friend from Centre York. What is the estimated cost of the whole canal when it is completed?
Of the whole Trent canal?
Of the Newmarket section.
The estimated ccst is in the vicinity of $600,000, I think.
Does that include storage dam and reservoir?
Yes.
How much of the $600,000 has been expended?
About $200,000 has been expended altogether.
Has the minister caused any inquiry to be made as to the possible tonnage on this canal? What is the tonnage arising from the town of Newmarket?
We have no such report. We have no such report on any part of the Trent canal although we are spending millions upon it.

Does not the minister think that in a case of this kind, where it is a branch of a canal, and not merely a link in^ the system, it would be advisable to ascertain the possible tonnage arising in that section ?

I have an engagement which will require me to leave after six o'clock. I thought that the hon. gentlemen would allow this item to go through and have any further discussion which they desire afterwards.
Let it stand.
What is the length of this section of the canal?
About ten miles.
Where does it start and end?
It starts in Cook's bay, Lake Simcoe and goes to Newmarket. I suppose you will allow this item to go through?
I think it is too serious to allow it to so through. I think the minister should allow time for further consideration as to the propriety of voting this money.

If the minister will take the Brockville * Recorder,' his own paper, and read the criticisms that were made with regard to an impovement that was made a few years ago on an important canal-the Rideau canal-when connection was made with the town of Perth he will see how determined was the opposition offered to that work. In the literature sent out every election reference was made to the expenditure on the Tay canal. It did not amount to half of the sum that my hon. friend proposes to devote to the digging of this ditch, and I am sure that when he comes to read his own paper and to reflect upon the speeches he has made condemning the government for having made that expenditure connecting the Rideau canal with the town of Perth he will withdraw this vote. If there ever was a useless expenditure proposed by the government this certainly is the most useless.

Residence of Yukon Commissioner, Dawson, $19,000.
This is to repair and to furnish the residence which was destroyed by fire some time ago.
How much did it cost altogether?
How much of that for furnishings?
Will this be let by contract and tender?

An estimate was made by the chief architect and it was thought better to have it done by days' work. There are not many contractors in the Yukon, I suppose, and besides it is difficult to let these repairs by contract.

Do we supply the Yukon Commissioner with a residence and furnish

it for him, and do we pay him a living allowance in addition to his salary of ?9,000?	*
I am not sure about the latter; I will inquire.
What was the estimate made by the chief architect?
$21,000 for the reconstruction of the building, but that di4 not include heating and fittings of various kinds and plumbing and electric wiring.
There is not much discrepancy there. Did the chief architect visit the place?
No. Our representative who examined the buildings made an estimate of the probable cost and that was passed upon by the chief architect.
Does the minister think it is a proper principle to furnish the residence of such an official as this?
I am not prepared to say to the contrary.

Unless the minister can say that this is a proper expenditure, we ought not to be asked to sanction it. It seems to me that the principle of providing residences and then furnishing them for officials is a very bad principle, except perhaps in the case of the) Speaker of the House of Commons and the Governor General.
Mr.! PUGSLEY. Why except these?
As far as the Governor General is concerned, it is well enough. I am not going to say that I particularly approve of the other, but I am not going to object to it because I have not made up mv mind.
What about the lieutenant governors of the various provinces?
I am not going to branch off to that question. The question I now propound to the minister is whether we should build a residence and furnish it for this gentleman. I submit that we should not.

If called upon to justify it, I would be quite prepared to do so, because it is in line with what has been the practice of, this country ever since confederation. The lieutenant governors of all the provinces have been furnished with residences and also with the furniture for them. That applies to every province of Canada except New Brunswick, where it was the case until along in the eighties, when the provincial government, led by the Hon. Mr. Blair, did away with the government house as an official residence. When the provinces came into the confederation all the government houses were fur- l
nished, and the renewals from time to time have been provided, not by the lieutenant governors themselves, but by the respective provinces. When Manitoba came into the confederation, a government house at Winnipeg was erected and also furnished by the federal government. In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta the government houses were also provided by the federal government. The Yukon is a territory of the Dominion, and in pursuance of the same line of policy the government house there was erected and furnished by the federal government. It must be borne in mind that a governor-and the commissioner of the Yukon is in the same position-holds his office only for a comparatively short period; and I presume that the reason for furnishing residences is that it would be a hardship on the governor to have to furnish a residence in the style in which he is supposed to live, because at the end of his term he would have to either sell his furniture or take it away with him, and his successor would have to furnish it all over again. I do not believe that I am called on to defend a practice which has always been recognized and held without question to be a reasonable and proper practice.
Did I understand the minister to sayl that the Dominion government built the government houses in Saskatchewan and Alberta?
Yes, when they were territories.
Has that been the case m the maritime provinces and Ontario?
Yes, they were all erected by the various governments before confederation. In Manitoba the government house was erected and furnished by the federal government.
Can the minister recollect the date when that was done?
Has the minister any recollection of a new government house in Ontario and Quebec or in any of the maritime provinces having been built by the federal government since confederation?

There have been no new government houses built in these provinces since ^ confederation, so far as I am aware. The lieutenant governors are occupying the same residences that were built and furnished by the various governments before confederation.

The reason I am asking the question is that in the province of British Columbia the government house, which I think was in existence before confederation, was burnt down a few years ago, and a new government house was erected at considerable cost by the provincial govern-

ment. Was any application made to the federal government in regard to that?
I am not aware of any.

In the event of an application being made by the provincial government to the federal government to be reimbursed and to be put on the same basis as the other provinces in this respect, I presume that a deaf ear would not be turned to them? Do I understand that the minister does not wish to answer the question?
I am not prepared to answer it.

It appears to me that the minister has not made a very strong defense of this item, in citing the cases of the lieutenant governors of the various provinces, and comparing them with that of a commissioner in a territory which yields a comparatively unimportant revenue.

Before proceeding with the reconstruction of this building the government made full inquiry, and I personally inquired as to the likelihood of the Yukon being a permanent mining district, and the information that I got was that owing to the very large expenditure which was being made by capitalists in introducing machinery for hydraulic mining and in view of the quartz discoveries, it was likely to be permanent, and that the wealth of the Yukon was very great. I conferred with Dr. Thompson, the representative from the Yukon in the last parliament, and he said that in his judgment, which I am sure would have great weight with those who knew him, from his knowledge of the country, he had not the shadow of a doubt that the district would be a permanent district, that there would be for all time a considerable population there and that it was in every respect desirable that the government house should be reconstructed. That had some weight with me, but it was not that alone which had weight, because I received information from other sources upon which I felt I could rely.
Is the minister not prepared to admit that the revenue in the Yukon now, is only about 20 per cent of what it was in 1901?
I know it has fallen off, but they are going into permanent mining, and it is expected that next year the output will approach the output of the most successful years.
Would the minister state the cost of the commission appointed to investigate into the cause of the fire? They reported that they were not able to ascertain the cost.

That report was made before I was minister and I have not the Mr. BARNARD.
statement with me to-night. I shall be glad to bring it down.

work.

In connection with this fenced off portion of Major's Hill Park, there is a monument inside of that fenced enclosure. mitted to continue there, as I understand it has continued for two years or more. The reason why the fence was put around the monument was that it might be protected from any defacement while the workmen were engaged in the construction of the new hotel. My own view is, and I am sure that members of the committee will agree with me, that while the work of construction is going on it is desirable that the monument be preserved from any possibility of defacement, and every person will see that it is proper that it should be inclosed by a fence until the hotel is completed, when the fence will, of course, be removed, and when we hope the monument will be in as good condition as it is at the present time.

I do not remember what was stated last session by others. Certainly I do not know that that was said by me.

The information I have is that the company intend to commence the construction of the hotel this spring. I had a letter from the vice-president of the company waiving some objections which he had to a clause in the deed which has been prepared by the Department of Justice, and asking that the conveyance should be completed as soon as possible with the view of Mr. LENNOX.
the company proceeding with the construction of the hotel.

This is for the whole telephone service of the various public buildings in Ottawa, including all the departments as well as the House of Commons.
