I see by the Auditor General's Report, at page V-108 that the price charged the government for telephones is $35. I understand that the regular price in Ottawa is $25.
I cannot tell the exact price; but I made inquiry last year, and my information is that the government _ gets telephones at the same price as private firms
I should think that taking so many they would get them for somewhat less than private individuals. Besides, many of them are used only for a portion of the year.
Where they are used only for a portion of the year I think there is a reduction.
I understand that the price for a residence telephone in the city of Ottawa is $25.
What is the office rate ?
I am speaking now of residences. I see that for a telephone in the residence of Mr. McDougald the charge is $35.

Is my hon. friend quite sure that the Ottawa rate for the residences of private individuals is $25 ? Because if it is, I would insist on the telephone company refunding. I certainly would not consent to pay more. I will make inquiry as to that.
My authority is a member who is paying that rate for a telephone in his residence in Ottawa, which ne is using the whole twelve months.

My information last year was the contrary of that, but my hon. friend having mentioned it, I will make it my business to look into it. I can assure the committee that we will not pay any more than is paid by private individuals.

Does the minister say that in paying out the public moneys of this country, he has never informed himself what rate the government is paying for telephones ? Does he have to ask members on the opposition side of the House what the rate is ? Instead of asking members what the rate is after he has paid the money, the situation ought to be reversed. The minister ought to be giving the House the information why he is paying $35 a year for telephones, apparently $10 above the rate any one else pays.
Does the hon. gentleman know that ?
I will assume the responsibility of saying that $25 is the regular Ottawa rate.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman; that is my own experience, and yet the minister pays $35 a year, and makes no objection. He asks us to pass the item and when it is questioned lifts his eyebrows and asks information from this

side. I think the information should come properly from that side.

I understand the rate for telephones in Ottawa for private residence is $25, but if that private residence has one boarder it is $45. The charge for an office phone is $35. Undoubtedly they have arranged a rate for the government offices. There must be some reason for paying $35.

Here is a case, Clerk of the Crown in Chancery residence, $35. I do not think the government should pay $10 extra for any boarders in the house of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Then Mr. McDougald, the Commissioner of Customs, pays $35. Does he keep boarders?
It is $20 in a boarding house.
I claim that the government should not pay more for phones in the residences of these officials than any private citizen would pay.
I quite agree.
The minister should see whether the government have been paying too much and make the telephone company refund.
The hon. gentleman has not told me yet of any individual resident in Ottawa who has one for less.

Mr. Porter and Mr. Perley each pay $25. These officials all have regular salaries and why should we make these extra expenditures? For the residence of the Minister of Finance they charge $50. Are they charging $25 extra for boarders that he keeps? He must have a lot of boarders. For the deputy minister, who does not keep as many boarders as the Minister of Finance, they charge only $25. For the private secretary they charge $40; he must have a boarder or two more than the deputy minister. In these cases the telephone company are not treating the government fairly and the Minister of Public Works should see that if the government are paying too much a refund is made.
Could not the minister bring down the facts?

I shall be glad to produce a statement of the amounts paid for different telephones in discussing the item ' miscellaneous expenditures '. When my attention was called to requests for telephones after I became minister I had inquiry made as to the charges for residences in Ottawa and I was informed that the rate given to the government was exactly the same as that given to private individuals. Of course we know that if there is a dupli-Mr. BOYCE.
cation of the service, a wall extension or a table extension, there is an extra charge, and this may be the case at the residence of the Minister of Finance. I have a table extension which is necessary if I am to have a telephone at all.

Last year $14,888 was paid for telephones in Ottawa alone. The minister will see that, in every case, where there is a telephone in the residence of an official, the charge is $35 per annum, except in the case of the ministers, where it is $50. I refer to the Auditor General's Report, page V-108. I see the telephone in the minister's house is charged $50. I do not know whether he is keeping boarders or not. The telephone in his messenger's house cost $35; the same with the census branch, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and others-in every case the charge is at least $35. In a few cases, like the ministers, they may require a telephone and an extension, but that is not required in the case of the messengers or most of these other officials. It seems clear to me that the telephone company are charging $10 more than they ought to charge.
I think the matter is one that ought to be inquired into. I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. _J. D. Reid) has called attention to it. I will allow the item to stand and make inquiries.
Will the minister answer my inquiry as to the principle on which this payment is made at all. Why should a telephone be paid for in the house of an employee ?

The theory is that these officials are liable to be called up on public business, and that it is not undesirable to allow a certain class of officials telephones in their residences. I think everybody will agree that it is reasonable that there should be telephones in the residences of the ministers as well as in their offices. I think the same would apply to the deputies and to the secretaries.
And the messengers ?

That is a question. It is a convenient thing for a minister to be able to call up his messenger to attend to a matter of public business. My own view would be that this would apply to one messenger in the department who would be liable to be called up at any time, but not more than one.
I should think the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery would not very frequently be called up out of office hours.
It is hard to discriminate.

I do not want the item to be held up, but I would like to have it understood that on some other item the

minister would explain exactly the position. And if I am right I want the minister to say that he will make the telephone company refund what it has been charging too much. And let us have the explanation.
I will undertake to do that.
How can the minister undertake to make them refund money paid in connection with a business transaction entered into with them ?
I did not say I would undertake to have them refund; I said I would undertake to give the explanation.
I understood the minister to say that if he finds the Bell Telephone Company have been charging $35 for a residence telephone when they charge others $25, he will make them refund the amount.
He goes back on that.
I want that understood.
My deputy tells me that, in the case of offices they charge $45 but the government have a flat rate both for residences and offices
The office telephones are charged here at $50.
I will undertake to have it looked into and get the information for the committee, and will give it when some other item is under discussion.

I understood the minister to say, both early in the debate and recently, that he would make the company refund any overcharge. And I was pleased to hear it. I think he should do that, particularly if this charge has been assented to under a misrepresentation. I will be glad to have him take that plank of the Conservative platform and enforce restitution.
If it appears, on full inquiry that the telephone company have charged more than they ought to charge, I think they ought to refund. I can only say I will look into it.

If any large corporation required as many telephones as the government do, I think they could get them at a more reasonable rate than the government seems to be paying. Since they promised to charge only $25, I think the minister will not be doing justice to the country if he does not cause them to refund the money. We have been held up in different parts of the country and told that public works could not go on, while money is being recklessly spent in Ottawa.

I find an item in the Auditor General's Report, page V-112, showing
that taxes paid on buildings rented by the government is a little over $11,000. That seems to be a new item.

The government rents a number of buildings in Ottawa, and, up to quite recently, these were regarded as being free of taxation under the British North America Act as they were occupied for Dominion purposes. I do not say that that is the reading of the Act. The Ontario government recently passed a law expressly declaring that such buildings should be subject to taxation. Outside the statute altogether, I should have thought it proper that taxes should be paid on buildings occupied by the government. I do not see why if a building is subject to taxation being rented by a private individual, the mere fact of it being rented by the government should enable it to escape taxation. At all events, the Ontario legislature has passed a law on the subject, and we have recognized the validity of that law and are paying taxes.

I do not object to the principle; I rather agree with the minister that it is right. But, when the government is-Tenting buildings in different parts of the city, merely because a change takes place-in the law of Ontario, I do not see why the-government should pay these large sums in taxation. It seeems to me the owners of the buildings should pay the taxes.
The hon. gentleman will see that the rental would be just that much higher.

It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to say that, but I don't agree with him. Here are properties in this city receiving very large rents, a new law comes into force that puts the taxation on the owner of the building, and does the hon. gentleman say that the government are going to assume this taxation? I think that, the government should see to it that the owners of these properties pay their own taxes.

On the other hand, if the government are going to pay the taxes, I think they ought to get the buildings at a less rental, because if the owner of the building rented it to any one else it would be taxed. The corporation of Ottawa is denied the privilege of that taxation. Now if the government commence to pay taxes it seems to me they should get a reduction in the rental.

That depends on circumstances. It seems in this case that the rental was fixed by the landlord on the theory that he would have no taxes to pay, he would charge so much as a net rent, based upon what he regarded as a fair return on his investment. That is usually the case. It is usually the cost of the pro-

perty and a fair interest on the amount invested which govern rentals. We do not think it is fair to compel the owner to pay taxes, because it would mean that he was getting much less for his property than he bargained for when he rented to the government. In the case of some other properties we agreed that we should pay the taxes.

The law in the province of Ontario, I understand is that where the landlord leases a property and there is no mention of taxes in the lease he is compelled to pay the taxes, and I am quite sure that it is the case under the government leases. I do not think it is fair, I repeat, that these property owners in the city of Ottawa who are receiving enormous rents for their properties, and where the government is spending large amounts of money, as they are in some cases, fitting up these properties, and when a change of law takes place, the government should assume all the taxes. It is unfair to the government, and it is a charge against the minister for defending it.
I think in mose cases the lease expressly provides that the government should pay what taxes there may be.
Perhaps the minister will produce one of these leases?
In addition to producing the lease, it will be necessary to bring down the assessed values of the properties, and a statement showing the amount of rent we are paying on each property.

I cannot bring down the assessed value of the property.

General did before-go away and leave us | with a lot of debts to pay.

The minister must have had some criterion uoon which he based this increase of $35,000-something more than a guess.
None of these things are guess work.

Then there is heating, taxes and so on. It costs about $50,000 for the rental of this building.
Yes, about that. That includes elevator attendance.
Well, take $42,000. The owner of this building receives $42,000 as a revenue and has nothing to pay out of it.
No taxes?
No, the taxes are paid by the government.
That is what I say.
That is straight rent. I do not believe that the building would cost an awful lot more than two or three times-
What would you call an ' awful lot ' ?

I estimate it in this I way. Let us see what the property is

assessed for. The assessors are sworn to assess these properties for what thev are worth. I understand that property in Ottawa is assessed -for its full value.
About two-thirds of its value I think.

This property is assessed at $118,000 so that at the minister's own estimate it would be worth $150,000, and $42,000 a year is an enormous rent. I think property owners in Ottawa are generally satisfied to get a rental of from 10 to 12 per cent of the value. How did the minister come to pay such a rental for this?
The lease was entered into before I became minister.
What is the term of the lease?
Five years, renewable at the option of the government.
When was it entered into?

Three or four years ago? The rental does seem high when you look at the total sum, but a fair way to determine its reasonableness is to remember that for this building you pay 56-14 cents per superficial foot and for the Trafalgar building which is owned by a private individual, 78 -08 cents per cubic foot. It is true that for the Imperial building we pay 34-07 cents per superficial foot, for the building occupied by the Interior Department 30 -06 cents per superficial foot, for the Seybold building 45-43 cents per superficial foot, but for the Corry building we pay 98 cents per superficial foot.

I have not the least doubt that the minister will find, if he inquires, that the rental of similar buildings on the same street is much less than he is paying. If I rent an office down town I may pay 56 cents per square foot on the exact number of feet in the room, but when this building was rented to the government they measured the halls, the elevator shaft, and everything else around the building.
How does the hon. gentleman know that?
It has been reported to me and the proof is that judging by the size of the building I do not believe you could figure out such a rental unless they measured the hall.
And the roof.
Yes, and the cellar as well.

The hon. gentleman has the unhappy faculty of assuming things to exist which do not exist in fact. The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken in saying Mr. J. D. REID.
that the corridors were included in estimating the area. We have the most correct measurement of every room in the building. If my hon. friend will inquire from any real estate man he will be told that 56 cents per square foot is a reasonable rent and very much less than is charged for other buildings. The building is equipped with elevators and modern conveniences and is fire proof, which is a very important consideration. I have it from the deputy minister whose duty it is when it is proposed to rent a building to inquire carefully into the rental value of other buildings, that the owners of the ' Citizen ' building on Spark street get $1 per square foot from their tenants.
Look at the difference of the value of land on Sparks street as compared with its value on the street where this building is.

But look at the fact that nearly 100 per cent more is charged for space in the * Citizen ' building than this building on Slater street, and I am inclined to think that for office purposes Slater street is pretty nearly as good as Sparks street although of course it would not be as good for stores.
What are the taxes on this building?
Dominion buildings-lighting, $125,000.
Are you over expending that vote this year and to what extent?

The actual expenditure for the present year to December 15 is $87,500, and to complete the fiscal year we estimate that it will take $35,000, making $122,500, with contingencies of $2,500, so that the actual experience of the present year is that it will take nearly $125,000. In regard to the buildings which are said to rent at one dollar per superficial foot, and so on, are they rented on the basis of the tenant paying for the heating, lighting, general fittings, furniture, and so on?
For that one dollar per foot the landlord does the heating and lighting.

Dominion buildings-power for running elevators, stamp cancelling machines, &c., $12,000.
Is this power for all the public buildings in Canada?
All except Ottawa.
What are these stamp cancelling machines?

They are used in the post office.
Dominion buildings-rents, &c., $200,000.

This item includes rents not only in Ottawa, but throughout the Dominion. It happens that in a number of towns where there is no public building, and which have arrived at the stage in their population and importance to make it desirable to have a post office, we rent a portion of a building and have it equipped as a post office.

In regard to this question of rents, while at1 first sight the manner in which they are calculated, according to the area of superficial feet, seems to be eminently fair, yet when we consider the comparisons suggested by the minister himself, we see how utterly unfair it is. In the one case we rent the room in the ' Citizen ' building, and have it heated and lighted, and have elevator service. In the other case I understand the government rent the entire building, and supply every service- heat, light and elevator-besides paying the taxes; and the ground value of the land is very much less. So that in every particular the comparison which the minister has advanced is eminently unfair. The only way in which you can get at a fair basis for rental is the one suggested by the minister himself, that all that a landlord can expect is a reasonable interest on the money invested, and the only way in which you can get at that is by ascertaining the assessed value of the building. In this case it is stated to be $118,000, on which a rental of $42,000 per annum is certainly a very high interest.

My hon. friend says that in order to institute a correct comparison we have to remember that the building on Sparks street, for which one dollar a foot is charged, heating and lighting are included. In order to make the comparison absolutely fair, I have added the taxes, heating, lighting and elevator attendance in the case of the Canadian building, and I find that it all amounts to only 71 -36 cents per square foot, which is about 30 cents per square foot less than is charged for the ' Citizen ' building on Sparks street.

If the minister wants to make a fair comparison, let him take the value of the land in the two cases, and he will find that on Sparks street it will be 10 or 15 times what it is on the back
street on which the other building is situated. The land value which is very important was left out of the calculation. I understood that the buildings occupied by the government were actually altered and fitted up by it and all repairs and expenses of every kind are borne by the government ; while in the * Citizen ' building or any other building the tenants would get rooms suitable for their purposes complete, and all these expenses would be borne by the landlord.

(Mr. Fisher) is not here, but perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) will ask that question when some item of the Department of Agriculture is under discussion.
Yukon public buildings - rents, repairs, fuel, light, water services and caretakers' salaries, &c., $80,000.
In the Auditor General's Report there are a number of items of charge for the commissioners residence which seem strange. I suppose the commissioner furnishes his own residence?
No, it is furnished by the government.
I see there is a charge for a sewing machine. Is that supplied by the government?
Perhaps that would be for hemming the curtains.
Telephone service costs $240.
That is where telephones cost money.
There is silver tea service-is the government supposed to furnish that?
Yes, the government furnishes the building; it belongs to the government and is available for the commissioner.
Can the minister tell me where, in the Auditor General's Report, I will find the figures showing what the water services under this item cost?
I have them here: Charges for water and ice; government house $500, Post office, $240; court house, $200.

Do rents not come down in the Yukon? There has been a great decrease in the population in the last five or six years, and one would think that liv-i*g would be cheaper, yet we appear to pay the same or an increasing amount.
Very little of this is paid for rent-I think the only item is $450. The total expenditure under this item up to November 26 last was $78,065.
You are going to have an over expenditure there.
Last year we had a vote of $85,000, so there will be still about $8,000 We may get through with that.

The Yukon is a portion of Canada where the revenue and population are decreasing, but the government expenditure there does not seem to decrease. Has the minister thought of applying his rule of economy to that territory?

As long as we keep up the administration of the Yukon these expenditures must be incurred. We cannot avoid such expenditures as those connected with the administration building, the government house and the court house. This includes also the salaries of various officers of the government at several mining recorders' offices. I agree that it is desirable to keep down the expenditures as much as possible in view of the fact that there has been a falling off in population. But I am inclined to think that the falling off is in the floating population, and that there is a permanent population in the Yukon which will continue, and probably increase.
What is about the permanent population ?

I understand in Dawson city there are 5,000 or 6,000, and in the Yukon altogether about 15,000 people. I understand that a wealthy company have been spending several millions of money in installing an up-to-date hydraulic mining plant, they have built a good many miles of canal system, and are going into mining on an extensive scale. That is in addition to the ordinary placer mining.

Before we take up another item, I would ask the minister to instruct his deputy to send us over, or leave with the clerk of public accounts, copies of those leases for that Canadian building. Would he leave them with the clerk of the Public Accounts Committee ?
I think we can hardly get them copied in time, but I will send a clerk with the originals, and give my hon. friend time to examine them.

Would the hon. minister allow me to say a word or two on harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia-as I
have to go away ?
Harbours and rivers-Nova Scotia, $279,310.

Some three years ago an item was put in the estimates for a wharf at Tatamagouche bay. During the by-election of 1907 there were $533 spent on this wharf. Last year another $1,000 was added to the appropriation to continue this wharf. I may say that last summer I got a letter from the engineer of the Public
Works Department at Halifax asking me to recommend a foreman to take charge of this expenditure of $1,000.
Did the hon. gentleman faint away when he got the request ?

I recommended a man whom I thought was an honest man, and after I had sent the letter of recommendation I got a reply stating that I did not have the recommending power, but that belonged to another gentleman. A few days ago I asked some questions in the House with regard to this wharf. I asked for what purpose this money was expended, and received the answer that it was in order that the inhabitants might get on to this island for fishing purposes. I also asked what the depth of water was at high and low tide, and I was informed that at low tide there was no water, and at high tide there was five feet. Now I am glad the minister has left this item out, because it was a waste of money, and there has been a lot of money'wasted in Nova Scotia. We want money spent down there on works that are useful rather than merely ornamental. I will send the minister a photograph of this beautiful wharf.
Harbours and rivers, New Brunswick- Beaver Harbour wharf, $10,000.

This consists of a revote of $5,000 and a new vote of $5,000 for the purpose of proceeding with the construction of a wharf at Beaver harbour in the county of Charlotte. This is a place of a good deal of importance and a wharf is very much needed. Its construction has been pressed for a number of years. It has now been undertaken and is under contract.
What is the contract price?
Will this complete it?
It is expected this will complete it.
Is that the wharf that was partly washed away or was put in the wrong place?
There was a provincial wharf which was partly washed away.
How did you spend all the money which was voted last year?
This is all a revote.
Then you have not spent anything?
Not yet.
But it was badly needed for several years?
When was the contract made?	j
The order in council was passed a short time ago and the contract must have been let within a week or ten days.
Was this one of the wharfs that the minister promised to the electors in the campaign?
There was a vote passed for this wharf last session. Parliament promised this last session.
Is there any revenue from this wharf?
There will not be until it is built.
Does the minister anticipate any revenue from this wharf after it is constructed and, if so, how much per annum?

I believe that this is a place of a good deal of importance. There are quite large industries there; among others, I think there is a large canning industry and I think that the steamer running between St. John and Charlotte county points call there. What the revenue will be it is quite impossible for me to tell. I am sure that no one will say that the construction of the wharf is not thoroughly justified upon public grounds.
The minister does expect some revenue?

Yes, when these wharfs are passed over to the Marine and Fisheries Department wharfingers are appointed and wharfage dues are collected.
Buctouche-channel through beach, $2,500.
Will the minister explain what this channel is for?
This is for the purpose of improving the harbour at Buctouche. There has been a large deposit of silt blocking the entrance to the harbour and this is to excavate a channel through the bar.
How much was expended last year?
W7as that done by day labour?
Yes.
Is this a dredging work?
Not a work done by an ordinary dredge but excavation work done by the day, using scrapers and shovels.
This is a channel through which water would pass so as to enable vessels to go in and out?
Yes.
Why is it not done with an ordinary dredge?
Because it is work which can be done by scrapers and horses at low tide.
What is the rise and fall of the tide?
I do not know, but I suppose it will be ten or twelve feet, will it not?
It would not be more than about six feet, I should think, up there.
This is to give a depth of three feet at low tide. If there is a tide of six feet it would give a depth of nine feet at high tide.

If you have a depth of three feet at low tide how can you do it without a dredge?
Mr. 'PUGSLEY. They can do it with scrapers very well.

I notice in the Auditor General's Report there is an account of an expenditure of $3,500 for the last fiscal year under the head of * Buctouche, N.B., Channel Through Beach.' I observe an item of * legal services, R. A. Irving, Buctouche, $122.10.' Would the minister explain what that was for?
I am unable to do so; I have not the memorandum here.
I notice there is a purchase of a site for $500. I would like to know whether this is in connection with the searching of the title. It seems a pretty good bill for a small property like that?
I will have that looked into.
I suppose that would be for a digger which would be operated by a steam winch.

Also I see that this barrister has been supplying stone as well as legal services for which he received $2.25 per cubic yard, amounting to $225. This appears to be a profitable undertaking for the Irvings.
That would depend on whether they were paid more than reasonable prices.
Does the minister know that they were reasonable?

I shall presume that they were in the absence of evidence to the contrary.
Campbellton deep-water wharf-extension, repairs, &c., $25,000.
Is this expected to complete this wharf?
I am unable to say whether this will complete as the chief engineer is unwell to-night and not able to be here.
We should ,know how much has been expended and how much it will take to complete.

The total expenditure at Campbellton to the 31st of March, was $150,514. The dredging cost $31,597 in addition, or a total of $182,139. The wharf is an extension 300 feet long and 45 feet wide; the dredging was required to give a depth of 25 feet at low water. It is crib work and done by contract.
Cape Bald breakwater, $15,000.
This is a new work which is very much needed.

What will be the total
cost?
It is estimated at about $32,000.
In what county is Cape Bald?

Westmoreland.
Cape Tormentine breakwater, $5,000.

How much will this work
cost?

The teredo worm causes great damage there and almost immediately after the brakewater was built, a number of years ago, repairs were found necessary from year to year. We are now using creosote timber.
Cummings Cove, Deer island, wharf, $23,000.
Will this complete?

Yes. It is new work; it will be done by public tender.
Dover-wharfs on Petitcodiac river, $3,000.
The total cost of this work will be $5,000.
Does the government build wharfs on the Petitcodiac river and pay the total cost of them?
Yes.
Then why is it that on the St. John river the governmeiit contributes only half the cost?	,

We have undertaken the building of a number of additional wharfs on the St. John river solely at
the expense of the government. The arrangement referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) was entered into when the Hon. Mr. Foster was Minister of Finance, and I do not know what reason there was for it.	,
It has been carried on for twelve years by your government?

Yes, except that we have extended quite largely the work which is done altogether at the expense of this government. In the estimates of .this year there is an amount of $20,000, which has never appeared before, for the purpose of building wharfs on the St. John river at the entire cost of the federal government.
Harvey bank-wharf, cribwork, $4,500.
Is this a new wharf?

Yes; it is to rebuild the old wharf. This is the total cost.
Heron island-wharf, $3,000.
Is this new?
No, it is to extend the wharf built by the provincial government.
What county is it in?

Restigouche. The estimated cost is $4,000.
ICouchibougouac harbour improvements, $3,700.
Will this complete the work?

Yes.
Lameque wharf-improvements, $2,500.
Will this complete?

This will complete the improvements.
Leonardsville, Deer island - reconstruction of wharf, $14,000.
This is to provide for the reconstruction of an extension of a wharf formerly built by the provincial government.
Will this finish the work?

Yes.
Lorneville breakwater-wharf, $29,000.

This will complete the work.
Mill's Point wharf, $3,800.
This will complete the payments.
What will the total be?
Was there a contract?

Yes. The contractor was Mr. Fawcett, who was the lowest tenderer.
Moncton wharf-enlargement, $16,000.
Is that the whole cost?
It may take a little more to finish it, but not very much more.
There was nothing done on that last year?
There was a commencement made by the contractor, bul difficulties have arisen, and we shall have to ask for new tenders under a somewhat changed plan.
Was the old wharf built by this government?
Yes, by the Railway Department. It is a railway wharf.
When were these tenders called for?
Last May or June.

In this connection I would like to remind the minister of a promise he made to some of the business men of Fredericton in regard to wharf accommodation there. I think that on the eve of the election he sent a telegram to a number of merchants in that city saying that he would do something toward the building of wharfs at Fredericton ; but I see that there is nothing for that purpose in the estimates. I would like to ask the minister why he is not carrying out that promise?

Mv attention was called to the desirability of assisting the city of Fredericton in giving wharf accommodation, and my hon. friend is quite right that I stated that I would recommend to my colleagues the taking of their request into favourable consideration. There is nothing in the estimates of this year, because that will be an entirely new work, and in accordance with our policy, we have postponed the construction of this wharf at Frederiction, as we have many other public works throughout Canada.
The minister, having said that he would take it into his favourable consideration, I suppose kept it in his favourable consideration until the 26th of October.
I have not changed my mind about it.
My we expect that this promise which the minister gave to the people of Fredericton will be carried out next year?

If my hon. friend will look at my promise, and bear in mind Mr. CROCKET.
what I said with regard to other public works, he will find that in due course my promise will be carried out.
Was the hon. gentleman in harmony with the government in that policy not to spend anything on new works in the coming year?
Of course, every member of the government is in harmony with the government in that.
How does that comport with the promise he made to the people down there that he would recommend the expenditure to his colleagues?
I never said that it would be done this year.

The hon. gentleman left the people with the impression that he. was going back to recommend this expenditure to his colleagues; then he comes here and says that his policy is not to do it. He is not in harmony with himself.
Are we to understand that the hon. gentleman sent a telegram during the election?

I sent either a telegram or a letter, and, whatever it was, I have no objection to it being produced, and I may say that I have no doubt that it was read at the council meeting in the very terms in which it was sent, without any alteration.
My hon. friend says it was read at a public meeting during the heat of the election?

I do not know that it was. It was not sent for that purpose. It was sent in response to a request from the mayor of Fredericton. I received a letter from the mayor, and I wrote a letter in reply; I do not think I sent any telegram. My letter stated my views, and those views I am prepared to stand by irrespective of what representative is sent by the county of York to this parliament.
My hon. friend will bring down the letter or telegram, I suppose?
If it is moved for, I will.
I understood the minister to state in his letter that he would recommend this appropriation to his colleagues. I would like to know if he has done that?
If my hon friend will produce the letter he will see what I stated.

The hon. minister said to-night that he had stated that he would recommend this appropriation to his col-

leagues, and I would like him to say whether he has done that. Mr. PUGSLEY. I stated that every new work for which tenders had not been called was postponed. That remark applies to a great_ many public works for which appropriations were made by parliament last session. My hon. friend can surefy understand that having postponed these works, I would not think of asking my colleagues this session to provide for works for which parliament had not already made appropriations and in respect of which nothing had been done. North Head, Grand Manan-breakwater wharf, $7,000. Mr. PUGSLEY. That is to continue that work. Mr. CROCKET. How much will it cost? Mr. PUGSLEY. A lot of the wharf was washed away in the great storm; it is expected to cost $46,000. Pink Rock, wharf, Shepody bay-extension, $5,000. Mr. PUGSLEY. That is to complete the extension. A contract will be let. Pointe du Chene-repairs to breakwater, $5,000. Mr. DANIEL. Are these repairs required on account of the teredo? Mr. PUGSLEY. Not to the same extent as at Cape Tormentine, but we are using creosoted timber to avoid the teredo. Mr. DANIEL. It would seem to be a waste of money to build a wooden breakwater if it is to be destroyed by the teredo. Mr. PUGSLEY. The Cape Tormentine breakwater was built a good many years ago, I think under the previous govern-inent, and we have to take it as we find it; it is the same with Point du Chene. Mr. DANIEL. Is creosoted timber an entire success in that respect? Mr. PUGSLEY. Pretty nearly a thorough success. Quaco harbour-part reconstruction and extension of east pier, $35,000. Mr. CROCKET. What is the amount of the contract? Mr. PUGSLEY. $32,900. The contractor is Mr. Charleson, of Ottawa. A part of the existing wharf was carried away and that will cost $2,000 to replace. Uiehibucto Cape-breakwater wharf, $10,000. Mr. CROCKET. Is this new? Mr. PUGSLEY. Yes. Mr. CROCKET. Have tenders been called for or a contract let?	Mr. PUGSLEY. Not yet. Some work has been done, we procured timber and began the work and have spent about $3,500 by day's labour. Richibucto wharf, $3,000. Mr. CROCKET. How much of last year's vote of $9,000 was expended? Mr. PUGSLEY. The whole of it will be expended. This is to repair a wharf bought from the municipality and another wharf which we bought. Mr. CROCKET. How much did you pay the municipality? Mr. PUGSLEY. We paid $5,000 for one and $1,500 for the other. Mr. CROCKET. To whom was the $5,000 paid? Mr. PUGSLEY. I think to Mr. Murray. Mr. CROCKET. Is that the manager of the Kent Northern Railway? Mr. PUGSLEY. I think so. Mr. CROCKET. And the government paid him $5,000 for a site for a wharf? Mr. PUGSLEY. For the wharf itself; it is an old wharf. Mr. CROCKET. Did the department have a valuation? Mr. PUGSLEY. Yes, by the resident engineer. His valuation was that the property had cost about $15,000. He said it was cheap at $5,000. He also consulted a prominent firm, Messrs. A. & R. Loggie, who informed him it was fair value. Mr. CROCKET. How long did Murray hold the title? Mr. PUGSLEY. Not many months. Mr. CROCKET. From whom did he buy? Mr. PUGSLEY. From Mr. CWLeary. Mr. CROCKET. For how much? Mr. PUGSLEY. $1,000. Mr. CROCKET. And the government paid $5,000 to Murray for a property that he bought in order to sell to the government at $1,000. Mr. PUGSLEY. I do not know that, the hon. gentleman is putting in something that is not so. Mr. CROCKET. But the minister knows that Mr. Murray bought the property during that season to sell to the government. Mr. PUGSLEY. I have learned recently that he bought the property. Mr. CROCKET. And the department paid $5,000 for that wharf just as Mr. Murray had bought it from Mr. O'Leary.
I do not know as to that.	.
The department paid $5,000 for it ?

Yes, on the representation of the engineer, Mr. Geoffrey Stead. It appears that it is a property of 500 feet frontage and considerable depth. Mr. Stead reported that it would cost $15,000 or $16,000 and was good value for $5,000. He did not report what Mr. Murray had paid for it. The department had no knowledge of what he paid. When it was brought to my notice what he had paid, I wrote to the engineer pretty sharply and ascertained the information on which he had reported as to the value of the property. He reported that the parties had wanted $10,000, which he thought too much, but, on going fully into the matter, he was confident that it was good value for $5,000, and so recommended the purchase.
Does the minister know that this very property was offered to the department for $1,000 ?
I know to the contrary. I have had a search made and find no record of any such offer.
To an officer of the department ?

I am not aware as to that. I am aware that Mr. O'Leary made the statement that he had offered it, not to an official of the department who had anything to do with wharf construction, not to the resident engineer, but to another official of the department who did not communicate with the department at Ottawa.
The gentleman to whom he says he made the offer is still in the employ of the department ?
But having nothing to do with wharfs. '______
Has the minister communicated with this gentleman, Mr. Water-bury ?
No.
Did the minister communicate with Mr. Murray in regard to the matter ?
No.
Are properties of this kind purchased by officers of the department without consultation with the minister ?
That is not customary, certainly.
Was the minister not consulted in this matter ?
The minister was consulted by the officials of his department.
Does the minister say he was not consulted by Mr. Murray ?
I have no knowledge of being consulted by Mr. Murray.
I would like to have the minister's own idea of the price paid for that property-does he think it was excessive ?

A few months ago my attention was called to the fact that the property had been purchased from Mr. Murray at a less sum than the government had paid, the sum mentioned being $1,000. I at once wired to my deputy to delay the completion of purchase until I had had an opportunity to make further inquiries. I received a telegram that the purchase had been completed through the Justice Department and the title had passed. I at once wrote to the resident engineer, Mr. Stead, calling his attention to what I had heard, and asking him to give me full particulars of the facts on which he relied in giving an estimate of the value. I also called his attention to the fact that the department had not been informed of the previous transfer and gave him direction that, in the future, I wanted him clearly to understand that whenever a property was purchased the department must be informed of all previous transfers in recent years so that we could form a judgment as to the value, and also any other facts that might assist the department in arriving at a full judgment. The engineer wrote me very fully and very frankly. He said he had heard that, some months before, the property had been purchased at $1,000. He regarded that as an absolutely ridiculous price for the property. He made inquiry and was led to believe that the previous owner had parted with it because he had no use for it, having other property. He also wrote that he had made inquiries of Messrs. A. and R. Loggie, who are among the most reputable business men in the lower provinces, or in all Canada, and they had instructed him that if they owned the property they would not think of parting with it for $5,000. He also reported that he had examined the property and the material in the wharf must have cost at least $15,000.
It wa3 all sawdust.

He says not. He says there is ballast of stone and gravel and probably a million cubic feet of cribwork, not new, of course, but a million feet must have cost a considerable sum. He said he could not get the property for less than he had, and that, in his opinion, the valuation was not a high valuation, but a low one.
Had the minister received any representation that this wharf was necessary ?
Yes.
From whom ?
From different people there.
Was there any public body in the county which made representations to the department ?

I cannot state as to that how. I know that we were urged to get additional wharf accommodation there. It appears that the Kent Northern Railway goes to the water, and there was no public wharf there, and the accommodation was very limited. There is no doubt we have a very valuable property and one that it was necessary we should have. In connection with the railway, it will be a great advantage to Richibucto.
How much is it intended to spend ?

$3,000 at present.
River St. John - including tributaries,
Will the minister state what he intends to do with this vote ?

This is a vote for blasting rocks, building wing dams and otherwise facilitating navigation of the river. I am inclined to think that we will expend a sum of money this year in improving Grand Falls. There are difficulties in the way of navigation so far as floating lumber is concerned. I think a few thousand dollars could be expended there with great advantage-right at the falls and a little above.
River St. John and tributaries-construction of wharfs in tidal waters, $20,000.
I would like the minister to state where he is going to build these wharfs.

I could not state exactly, but we have applications for quite a number of wharfs, both in the counties of Queens and Sunbury, and some in the county of Kings. There is one at Oromocto, another at Scotchtown, and another I think at Burton. There aro quite a number which are urgently required in the public interest. I will get a list later if the hon. gentleman wishes.

The minister stated some time ago that many public works had been proposed but had to be abandoned, but he did not intend to abandon those which came under one of three categories, and one of those categories was cases where tenders had been called for. Now, I wish to remind the minister that tenders were called for no less than nine wharfs in the county of Queens and Sunbury. I have here a clipping from the ' Daily Telegraph ' of St. John, dated October 13, 1908, which reads thus:
Nine new wharfs in Queens and Spnbury-
On representation of Colonel McLean, Minister of Public Works calls for tenders-
List of places where wharfs will be built.
The Department of Public Works, Ottawa, as will be seen by reference to another column, are calling for tenders for nine new wharfs in Queens-Sunbury. These will prove of great benefit to the residents of the localities and have been procured-
They had already been procured.
-through the representations of Colonel H. H. McLean, the Liberal candidate in Queens-Sunbury, to Hon. Mr. Pugsley, Minister of Public Works.
This was dated 13th October, little less than a fortnight before the elections.
The places where the new wharfs will be located are as follows:-
The Range, Parish of Waterborough, Queens county, N.B.
Burton, Parish of Burton, Sunbury county, N.B.
Newcastle, Parish of Canning, Queens county, N.B.
Barker's, Parish of Sheffield, Sunbury county, N.B.
McAllisters, Parish of Chipman, Queens county, N.B.
Young's Cove, Parish of Waterborough, Queens county, N.B.
lronbound Cove, Parish of Chipman, Queens county, N.B.
Scotchtown, Parish of Canning, Queens county, N.B.	,
Lower Jemseg, Parish of Cambridge, Queens county, N.B.
Tenders for these wharfs will close on November 12.
As tenders had been called for in respect to all these wharfs, I think they should be included in the estimates of work to be done this year. I have here a copy of the advertisement:
Tenders for wharfs on St. John river and Grand Lake, N.B.
Then it gives the nine places I have just read. That advertisement is signed by 'Nap. Tessier, Secretary.'
Does my hon. friend say that he approves of my going ahead with these wharfs ?
Certainly, I do.
Well, I intend to do so.
Then why are they not included in the estimates ?
I have got a vote of $20,000, $5,000 more than last year.
Will that build nine wharfs?
It should.
Is my hon. friend the member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) satisfied with that?
$20,000 is pretty good.

I am speaking on behalf of the people of Queens and Sunbury, who, I was afraid, had been deluded by these promises made previous to the election. I call the attention of the minister to the fact that these promises have been made, and naturally the people expect him to carry them out.

I am delighted that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) is giving me his assistance in obtaining these necessary public works. I am also highly pleased to hear him state this evening that he thoroughly approves of the policy adopted by the Minister of Public Works in erecting these wharfs, because I understand he joins with me in believing that these wharfs are absolutely necessary for the proper navigation of the River St. John. But I want to remind my hon. friend that he has changed his opinion this session from the opinion he held last session. I want to remind him that when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) stated on the floor of this House that it was a vicious principle to erect at the pub-lie expense wharfs in rivers or lakes, and that the public money should only be expended on wharfs in harbours or on the sea coast, my hon. friend heard that statement and he did not dispute it.
I never heard the hon. member for North Toronto make any such statement, either in this House or out of it.

I have an extract to prove what I say, and if my hon. friend wishes I will give it to him, because I used that extract in speeches in the county of Queens and Sunbury and I used it on nomination day. The statement cannot possibly be denied. As regards the statement made by my hon. friend that he was not present when the hon. member for North Toronto made that statement

1 was only endeavouring to answer the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel). I am glad to know that he thoroughly approves of the principle laid down by this government and that is that every necessary public work, every necessary wharf in tidal waters and in navigable waters, will be constructed at the expense of the government of Canada. I was also delighted to know that this principle meets with his approval and, of course, meets with the approval of all hon. gentlemen of the opposition. I want also to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that this principle has been opposed in this House by hon. gentlemen on the opposition side. It has been opposed by the hon. member for North Toronto and by other speakers on his side. I also desire to say that we give credit to the Minister of Public Works for inaugurating that principle and carrying it forward.

I am very pleased to hear the remarks of my hon. friend. Although he was a little inexact in some of his statements I quite exonerate him from any intention of being wilfully inexact. But I would like him and the members of this House to understand that in so far as I am concerned I am entirely in accord with any government that provides proper means for transportation and the carrying on of the business of this country whether it is on the sea coast or on the inland lakes and rivers. I never lifted my voice against the expenditure of money for any such laudable purpose and I do not propose to. I shall not do so for one reason, that, in the city, that I come from, we are looking for some expenditure for purposes connected with the great transportation interests of this country. I would not feel like advocating expenditures for that purpose in my own constituency if I were not willing to advocate them in |the constituencies of other hon. gentlemen whether on this side of the House or not. While my hon. friend from Queens and Sunbury would like to have imparted a little irony or sarcasm into his remarks I do not think they apply in any degree whatever to the member for the city of St. John.
Has the department made an estimate of the cost of these nine wharfs in Queens and Sunbury before calling for tenders.

The department prepared plans and called for tenders which we thought would be the best guide as to what these wharfs should cost, but, when the tenders came in, with respect to several of them, we thought that the price was too high and we also thought that the plans might be simplified so as to reduce the cost very materially. My own view, based on an experience of a good many years in connection with the building of wharfs on the St. John river when I was a member of the provincial government, is that we ought to get suitable wharfs on the St. John river at a cost of from $1,200 to $3,000. We are now having new plans prepared with the view of getting a cheaper wharf, one which will answer all practical purposes just as well and we hope to get the cost of the construction of these wharfs down to from $1,200 to $3,000, according to the length of the wharf, the depth of the water and the difficulty in making the approaches to the wharfs.
What was the total amount of the tenders that were received?
They ranged between different amounts. Some were as high as $7,000,	*
On the plans that had been drawn?
Yes, that fliad been drawn by the engineers at St. John. We thought the cost was greater than suitable wharfs should cost and we gave directions to reduce and simplify the plans.
After the elections were over the plans were simplified.
The minister did not state whether he intended to build these wharfs or not.
That is the object of the vote.
And it is expected to build them?
Yes.
Is the work to be done on all these wharfs during the present year?
We hope to be able to proceed with the work on all of them as soon as we can get the plans and have the tenders called for.
What county are these in?
Queens-Sunbury and King's.
How many wharfs are there in the county of Queens-Sunbury?
My hon friend from the county of St. John read the list. We hope to construct all of these.
That will be nine in one county.	.
There are two counties.
We are to understand that nine wharfs are to be constructed in one constituency represented by my hon. friend?
That is right but the water stretches are very large. They take in St. John river, Grand lake and Wash-demoak lake.
All on the recommendation of my hon. friend?
On the request of the hon. gentleman on the urgent request of the people in the various localities.

Was the Minister of Finance consulted about these large expenditures?
Mr. FIELDING- These nine wharfs seem not to be very extravagant in their cost. I do not think that even the whole amount of the tenders represents a very extravagant expenditure. I think it is within the reasons of economy that have been laid down.
River St. John-wharfs in tide water-contribution to the local government not to exceed one-half the first cost of wharfs built by it, $5,000.
Are you buying wharfs from the local* government or what?

I would like, with the consent of the committee, to strike out the words ' River St. John ' because for some reason or other, the contribution to be made to the provincial government is limited to wharfs in the tidal waters of the river St. John. The provincial government have built a wharf upon a tidal river in the northern part of the province and they have urged that we should pay one half the cost of it. I do not see why the rule was limited to the St. John river. It is better for us where we can, to get the provincial government to see its duty to pay one-half the cost rather than that we should pay the whole of it. I move that the words ' River St. John ' be struck out. It does not add to the liability but enables us to distribute it to other rivers.
It just takes that much away from the River St. John?
It may.

As a representative of one of the St. John river counties I object most strenuously to the proposition of the minister. Last session other representatives of these river counties as well as myself protested that these counties were not treat-

ed equitably in regard to the appropriations for wharfs. We pointed out that there were thousands and thousands of dollars spent upon the rivers in the province Of Quebec-the Saugenay river was especially instanced-where this government paid the entire costs of the wharfs and that on the important river St. John the government contributed only one-half the cost. The decision of the Minister of Public Works now to interfere with that pittance is an injustice to the people of these /"'unties. . I strenuously object to the proposition of the minister which will result in reducing the appropriation for the River St. John. I have pointed out that this government has paid the whole cost of the wharfs on the Petitcodiac river, and it is certainly very strange that after his professions of generosity to-night the minister should now propose to reduce even the beggarly half-cost contributions to the construction of wharfs on the river St. John. If the minister wants to aid the construction of wharfB in other parts of the province then his proper course would be to take an extra appropriation for that purpose and not divert money that has always been applied to the St1. John river. It is the dutv of the government to nav the whole cost of the wharfs on tidal rivers in the province of New Brunswick as they do in all other provinces of the Dominion.

The striking out of the words ' River St. John ' will not in any way affect the money that would go to the St. John river. For the first tipe in the history of the country we have a vote of $20,000 for wharfs on that river. This is purely a question between my department and the government of the province of New Brunswick, because unless they build the wharfs we cannot contribute half the cost. The provincial government through the Chief Commissioner of Works has requested me to change the wording of this resolution and I would ask the committee to allow me to do so.
Is this in the nature of a subsidy for wharfs already built?
We pay one half the cost of the wharfs which the provincial government has built.

How is it that when the provincial government of British Columbia applies to this government for a subsidy for works which are usually subsidized by the federal government the answer made to British Columbia is that there is constitutional objection to paying subsidies to any provincial governments; that they can only pay subsidies to private owners, but when we come to the province of New Brunswick (the minister's own province) we find that another yard stick is applied and that there the Federal government can Mr. CROCKET.
pay subsidies to the provincial government, when there is, it is said, a constitutional obstacle to paying them to the provincial government of British Columhia. That is a matter which ought to be explained.

The hon. gentleman has been misinformed. The Dominion government has contributed one-half the cost of works upon the Fraser and Columbia rivers when those works would not ordinarily fall to the federal government, they not being connected with navigation. But by reason of the importance of the work and the extent of the damage that otherwise would be done, this government has on more than one occasion actually contributed one-half of the cost of protection works in the constituency of my hon. friend. I have never heard this government raise the constitutional objection that it could not assist a provincial government with regard to works towards which the federal government might fairly contribute. Some fifteen years ago the Dominion government agreed to contribute one-half the cost of the wharfs on the tidal waters of the St. John river which the government of New Brunswick might build. That practice has been continued all these years and all the New Brunswick government asks now is that, instead of paying this amount to them for wharfs on the St. John river, it may be extended to other tidal rivers.
If the minister makes the change he proposes, does he not think he ought to increase the amount of the appropriation?

The Minister of Public Works has, as usual, an ingenious answer to the question I put, but his answer does not meet the case at all. In the instances on the Fraser river to which he has referred the Dominion government did very reluctantly and after a great deal of pressure make contributions towards works which we claimed in British Columbia we were not responsible for. but to which, in our devotion to the public interest, we consented to contribute one-half in order to avoijd the damage to property that would have been caused by the neglect of the federal government to do their plain duty upon the Fraser river. The federal government resisted the Claim we made, and in every instance in which they helped us on the Fraser river they repudiated responsibility and stated they did so as an act of grace and not as a matter of right. Why, no later than to-day, in answer to an application I made to the Department of Public. Works for the continuation of certain wofks which we were able to get this government to undertake on the Fraser river at Langley, the minister sent me a letter over his own signature entirely repudiating any responsibility for the work which his

department had undertaken and left in an incomplete state. He stated in his letter to me that this work was a matter of provincial and not Dominion concern. When I said that he had one yard stick for British Columbia and another yard stick for New Brunswick I referred more particularly to the doctrine laid down by this government in connection with the bridge over the Fraser river at New Westminster. The answer to our application for a subsidy was that if we would hand over that bridge to a private corporation to exact toll from the people of the Fraser valley for ever, then this government would give a subsidy amounting perhaps to $300,000 for the bridge, but because it was owned by the province, and we proposed to keep it in the public ownership of the people of the province, this government had not a cent to give us. They told us that there was a constitutional objection to giving any bonus to the province except a bonus authorized by the several Acts of confederation, while now we find them giving a direct subsidy to the province of New Brunswick towards the creation of public works. I am not objecting to that subsidy, but I am objecting to one rule being applied to the provinces of eastern Canada and another rule to our disadvantage being applied to the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In regard to the amendment proposed, I fear it might mean a change in the destination of the vote, and I am not sure of the right of the committee to make a change.

In that case I withdraw the motion.
River St. John-survey between Fredericton and Woodstock, with a view of improving navigation, $5,000.
There was an appropriation of $5,000 for this last year. Is that all expended?
Yes.
And this is an additional $5,000 to continue the work or to pay for the work already done?
To pay some balance, and to continue the work.
Can the minister say how much the survey of September and October last cost the country?

The expenditure to November 30, 1908, was $2,976.27. We expect that the further expenditure, I suppose for the payment of the balance, will be $2,023.63. The accounts are not all in yet. That would make a total of $5,000 expended before the close of the fiscal year. The surveys are not entirely completed, and we want to continue the work.

If not out of order, I would like to call attention to a statement which I understand was made on the hustings during the election campaign in regard to that survey by the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket). He said:
The Grits had had several fake surveys on land up and down the valley of the St. John; but now they were making a fool survey on water.
I would like the hon. member to state what he means by a fake or fool survey.

If the hon. member for Kings and Albert will consult his friend, the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell), I think he will be able to gratify his curiosity as to what was meant by the references to the ' fake survey of the land ' and also to the ' fool survey of the water.' The hon. gentleman no doubt still has a recollection of the survey for the Transcontinental railway which was conducted along the banks of the St. John river during the election campaign of 1904 and of his strong denunciation of the character of that survey at the last Liberal convention at St. John. On that occasion the hon. member for Carleton declared that the survey was no survey at all, that there was not so much as even a profile of it to represent the thousands of dollars which it cost the people of the country. This is what I called and what the people of the St. John valley called ' the fake survey.' The expression seemed to sum up the views of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) in short metre. I hope my hon. friend from Kings-Albert now understands the reference. As to the fool survey of the water that was applied to the survey of the river between Fredericton and Woodstock which was made in a tow-boat during the last campaign under the management of a young man named A. E. Hanson, and which the minister has informed us will require another five thousand dollars in addition to the five thousand dollars which was voted last year to pay the bills.
I would like to ask the hon. member if it was not at the request of two Conservatives, Shaw and Bull, that this dredging was to be done?
I am not aware.
I am informed that the hon. gentleman is aware of that fact.

As I do not have any public works in my constituency, and do not ask for any, I did not suppose that I would have to take a hand in these debates about public works in New Brunswick. But as the hon. mmber for York (Mr. Crocket) seems to be somewhat excited over this matter of the survey of the River St. John,
I would like to point out to him, what I have pointed out within a year in this

House, that this survey of the St. John river was done at the request of a public meeting in Woodstock, attended by a number of influential people from his own constituency, including the board of trade from his own city, who came to Woodstock, and joined the board of trade of that town in passing a resolution asking me to use my influence with the government to have this survey made in order to ascertain if it would not be possible to have water communication between Woodstock and Fredericton during a longer period of the year 1 brought the matter before the Minister of Public Works and his department, and they went into it; and I think it comes with poor grace from the hon. member for York to refer to this as a fake survey. No man knows better than he does that there never was a more genuine attempt made to secure a public improvement. The hon. gentleman has referred to Mr. Hansen, who was employed in the work. He would not say to Mr. Hansen's face what he has said tonight; and he would not say with regard to another gentlemen-and a good Conservative at that-Mr. Miles, who was employed on that survey, what he has said to-night; and I do not think he would say in his own constituency what he has said to-night.
It was the hon. member lor Kings and Albert who stated that I had said it.	i U

It is not very often that we bother calling the hon. gentleman down, but there are times when even the patience of a long-suffering man like myself is exhausted. My hon. friend knows the necessity of that work. He knows that if we succeeded in demonstrating to this government that we could extend the water communication down the river St. John three or four months in the year, it would be one of the greatest boons that could be conferred on that part of the province. I happen to know the nature of the report of one of the gentlemen who made this survey, and he is very hopeful that navigation to a depth of eight or nine feet can be obtained by the expenditure of a very small amount of money. I commend the Minister of Public Works for continuing, this investigation, and hope he will succeed in demonstrating that by dredging the river we can have at a reasonable cost the navigation we desire. While my hon. friend from York may not wish to see anything done by this government that will gain credit for it in the eyes of the people, I can assure him that if the Liberal representatives from New Brunswick can do anything to benefit the people, we will do it, regardless of whether the hon. member from York likes it or dislikes it.

I believe that when this vote was proposed last year, the hon. member from Carleton made a statement Mr. CARVELL.
somewhat similar to the statement he has made to-night in regard to the proposal of this survey being made by the boards of trade of Woodstock and Fredericton. It is quite true that these bodies were very much interested in the improvement of the navigation on the St. John river between Fredericton and Woodstock. I urged that matter several times in the House; but that was the first intimation we had that these boards of trade or any responsible people had asked of this government to make an appropriation of $5,000 or $10,000 to survey the water between Fredericton and Woodstock. I think that the members of the Fredericton Board of Trade will be very much surprised to learn it. There are eight or ten places in the river where dredging is required, and these were just as well known as the post offices along the river. I had correspondence myself with the Public Works Department, which show that they have had for years reports on the matter, sent in by Mr. Shewan, of St. John, a competent authority, these reports gave the department all the inforamtion that could possibly be attained or that was reasonably necessary for the purpose of determining what appropriations would be necessary. I do not withdraw one word of what I said with reference to the perfect foolishness of this vote. It was the subject of laughter during the election campaign wherever referred to by the people living along the river and the people in Fredericton, Bo much so that the gentleman in charge to whom my hon. friend has made reference, became known to his friends as the hydro-grapher. The money was expended, and that seems to be the only object to whom my hon. friend has made reference. If we had one or two of the bars and obstacles dredged from the channel between Fredericton and Woodstock, we would have had some benefit from the expenditure, but to pay out such a sum in such a moment, for the purpose of getting information that the department has and has had for years on the file, is certainly the height of folly.

The hon. gentleman has only to talk about five minutes to show his absolute ignorance of the subject under discussion. When the work started and the engineers got their instructions from the officials in St. John they were directed to do the very thing, he has advocated, to take ten or twelve spots along the river and make a report. I recommend a prominent engineer and he spent a week on the work. He then said: I might as well stop the work and save money unless I am allowed to make a thorough survey and give information of some value. He said that if, he surveyed the six or seven places pointed out to him they would have no knowledge of the condition of the river between these two points, would not know whether there were three feet .or sixteen

feet, and at his solicitation I took up the matter with the Minister of Public Works and orders were given to make a thorough survey. It is just as well that my hon. friend and the people should know this. I have seen the plans and profile of the upper 25 or 30 miles of that work and there are three or four dozen places in this 24 miles that required the survey without which the department would have no knowledge on which to come to the conclusion as to the dredging of the river. If my hon. friend would spend as much time trying to find out /the facts of each case, as in reading a paper called the ' Gleaner,' published in Fredericton, which throws insulting terms at everybody employed by this government to do anything, he would know more about the subject than he has given evidence of to-night.

Has it ever occurred to my hon. friend to have a branch of the Trent Valley canal built down the St. John river?
St. Andrews wharf, $18,000.
What will be the total cost?
Was any work done last year?

No, the contract is just being let.
St. John harbour-improvements, repairs, renewals, $25,000.
What does the minister expect to do with that?
The ordinary work that goes on, of repairing a breakwater and other work which might not be considered as a part of the national work. There is work at the Partridge Island pier.
Has this anything to do with the work of the dredge 'Fielding?'

No.
Seal Cove, Grand Manan island-breakwater pier, $32,000.
Is that a new work?

Partly. It is to extend the breakwater, part of which was swept away in the great storm.
Shippegan harbour-improvements in Ship-pegan gully, $3,500.

There was an expenditure of $5,691 on this account last year. Among the items I see Loggie, W. S., rope, $21.89; spruce, $17; shingles, $13.75; hardware, $75.04, a total of $127.43. Is that the hon. member for Cumberland?
I would suppose that must be some mistake because W. S. Loggie is not carrying on business. There is the W. S. Loggie Co.'y, Limited.
Is Mr. Loggie a part of it?

Yes, the company was incorporated twenty years ago.
Whitehead, Grand Manan wharf, $5,400.
I think that will complete it.
Is there a contract or is it day's work?

A contract, $4,851.
Welchpool (Campobello island) wharf, $24,000.
This is another item that looks large to us in British Columbia who get appropriations in such small chunks.

My hon. friend speaks of small chunks. Look at the improvements on the Fraser river. The hon gentleman forgets all these. The total probable cost of the wharf is $24,000. This is a very important wharf, as a large business is done at Campobello. The wharf will have a length of 314 feet, measured on the centre line, with a stone approach. It will be built of ordinary cribwork. We called for the tenders and the lowest tender has been accepted. I am satisfied, from the report of the engineer, that the price is fair and reasonable.
Is this work being built of creosoted timber?
No.
Why not?
Because the teredo worm is not so harmful along the Bay of Fundy coast as in some other places.
I am confident that the minister is mistaken about that. In East-port, Maine, the wharfs are very seriously injured by the teredo.
I do not think that such is the case along the Charlotte coast. The hon. gentleman knows that the teredo is not injurious in the St. John harbour.

The fresh water running into St. John harbour makes it impossible for the teredo worm to live there, as it lives only in salt water. But in the Bay of Fundy, and around Grand Manan, I am confident the teredo is injurious. The minister seemed to think he had made such an improvement over the former government's policy by using creosoted timber, that I thought he would not use anything else in this case.

We are not building with creosoted timber around the Bay of Fundy.

I think my hon. friend is mistaken as to the destructiveness of the teredo worm there.
The teredo is at Eastport. and if it is there it is in the harbours of Grand Manan.
The minister overlooked my question. I congratulate the people of Welch Cove on this wharf. But I would like to know, for purposes of comparison, how big a place it is.

The absurdity of that question would be apparent even to my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Taylor) if he knew where Welch Cove was. This harbour is on an island in the Bay of Fundy, whose only means of communication with the mainland is by vessel. The wharf will be used by many more than merely those at the place where the wharf is built. The wharf is very necessary in the public interest.

I have to thank the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) for the courtesy he has shown in addressing this lecture to me, and for the language with which he opened his polite address. But, while I appreciate his kindness, I would like to renew my question to the minister who has charge of this appropriation. I ask the question because I desire information. I could lecture the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) to more effect, perhaps than he can lecture me. But that is not the purpose of this committee. I am addressing what I believe to be a proper question to the Minister of Public Works, and I think I am entitled to the information, for purposes, as I have said, of comparison.

At Welch Pool Cove, where the wharf is built, there is a population of about 600. Campobello is a very rich island, and one to which many people resort in the summer. There are two large summer hotels. The town has a number of stores, a lobster cannery employing 25 hands, and a boneless herring cannery employing 50 hands. Besides the summer hotels, there are many summer cottages, mainly occupied by people from the cities of the United States. Five steamers call there and a number of sailing vessels make Campobello their headquarters.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will resume in supply, the Postmaster General presenting his estimates. If these be finished the Minister of Public Works will resume.
